stories.headline: Banks poised to post colossal profits buoyed by higher interest rates just as Healey eyes bumper windfall tax
stories.claim: Chancellor John Healey is reportedly preparing a windfall tax of around £7bn on UK banks in his October Budget.
stories.summary: Reports say Chancellor John Healey is considering a roughly £7bn windfall tax on UK banks ahead of his first Budget on 28 October. The big four lenders posted £29bn in pre-tax profits in the first half of 2026, lifted by higher-for-longer interest rates. The proposed package would include restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, worth about £2bn, plus changes to how losses on quantitative easing reserves are accounted for, worth at least £5bn a year. UK Finance warns that higher taxes could cost the economy nearly £20bn over ten years.
key_points: The big four banks (Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays, HSBC) made £29bn pre-tax profit in the first six months of 2026, up more than a fifth year on year.
Healey is reportedly poised to target banks in his first Budget on 28 October, a target of about £7bn a year.
Restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8% would raise about £2bn; deferring QE reserve losses could save at least £5bn a year by 2030, per IPPR.
UK Finance warns a higher surcharge could cost the economy nearly £20bn over a decade, mostly outside London.
Higher government borrowing costs have eroded half of the £24bn headroom the Chancellor has to balance the books.
stories.story:
The Times-style reporting in This is Money says the banking sector is braced for a fresh tax raid from Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget, due on 28 October. The report notes that the big four banks, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and HSBC, made combined pre-tax profits of £29bn in the first half of 2026, more than a fifth higher than a year earlier. These gains have been helped by interest rates staying high for longer, which lets lenders charge borrowers more than they pay savers.

The most straightforward option under consideration would be to raise the bank surcharge on profits back to 8% from the current 3%, a level cut by Jeremy Hunt in 2023. That would reportedly raise about £2bn. A think-tank, the Institute for Public Policy Research, has suggested a second measure: changing how the Treasury accounts for losses on banks' reserves held at the Bank of England under quantitative easing. The IPPR estimates this could save at least £5bn a year by the end of the decade without affecting bank profits or monetary policy. Together, the measures would bring about £7bn a year.

UK Finance, the trade body, has argued that a higher surcharge could cost the economy nearly £20bn over ten years, with most of the lost output outside London, by reducing lending and investment. Healey recently praised the banks as part of the country's economic strengths, shortly before the reported plans emerged. Lenders are described as politically easy targets because of their taxpayer bailout after 2008.

The report also notes that higher government borrowing costs have already used up half of the £24bn-a-year fiscal headroom the Chancellor has. Barclays updates investors on nine-month profits this week and Lloyds reports a day after the Budget. None of the measures has been officially announced, so the final shape of any bank levy remains uncertain.
stories.likelihood_reason: Reported by a mainstream personal finance outlet citing expected Budget plans and a think-tank proposal, but no official announcement has been made and the scale is uncertain.

No official government confirmation yet
stories.market_take: Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and HSBC could see pressure on shares if a bank levy is confirmed in the Budget.

stories.headline: ‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
stories.claim: Housing and living-cost protests spread from Spain and France to Milan, Lisbon and Albania, with violence and arrests reported.
stories.summary: Protests over housing costs and living expenses have spread from Spain and France to Italy, Portugal and Albania. In Milan, a Saturday march turned violent, with about 50 people detained and at least two police officers injured. In Lisbon, protesters set up a tent camp in Rossio Square demanding action on housing. Italy's prime minister Giorgia Meloni blamed 'hooligans' for the violence, while Portugal's government said it understood public anger. Albania has seen violent demonstrations over university fees and calls for the prime minister's resignation.
key_points: A Saturday march in Milan over living costs turned violent, with masked rioters throwing stones and setting fire to barricades.
Police used water cannon and teargas in Milan; about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, were detained and two officers injured.
In Lisbon, hundreds stayed overnight at a tent camp in Rossio Square, following a nationwide march of thousands.
Portuguese housing prices rose 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice the EU average, according to official data.
In Albania, protests over university conditions and tuition fees turned violent, with police using rubber bullets for the first time.
In Spain, a snap general election has been called for late November after housing measures were voted down in parliament.
stories.story:
Protests over the cost of living and housing have spread beyond Spain and France into Italy, Portugal and Albania, in some cases turning violent. In Milan, a march against rising living costs that began peacefully ended with masked people throwing stones and paving blocks at riot police and setting fire to barricades made of bar tables. Police responded with water cannon and teargas, and at least two officers were hurt. The LaPresse news agency reported about 50 detentions, many of those held being minors. Prime minister Giorgia Meloni said the right to protest did not extend to setting cities alight and accused hooligans of exploiting the demonstrations. Milan's centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said the grievances were understandable but the violence was not justifiable.

In Lisbon, a tent camp similar to one set up in Madrid weeks earlier appeared in Rossio Square after a nationwide march drew thousands. Protesters said they were struggling with rents and housing costs. Official data shows Portuguese housing prices rose 124% between 2015 and 2024, about twice the EU average. Portugal's prime minister, Luís Montenegro, said his government understood public frustration but warned rivals against importing unrest seen in France. A protest camp in Porto had already been set up earlier.

In Albania, demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of prime minister Edi Rama. Protesters threw rocks and petrol bombs, torched cars and set buildings on fire, including a court, banks and a post office. Police used rubber bullets for the first time in the protests, which follow months of anti-government demonstrations.

The unrest traces back to Spain, where an 87-year-old woman was evicted after failing to pay a 230% rent increase, sparking protests and a camp in Madrid. The government's emergency housing measures were voted down in congress, and prime minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for late November. In France, a movement that began over school conditions has grown into a nationwide protest against inequality, with more than 1,200 people arrested on Saturday. Whether these protests widen further or fade will depend largely on how governments respond to housing and living cost pressures.
stories.market_take: Broader political unrest in Europe could weigh modestly on sentiment towards euro-area bonds and property-linked shares.

stories.headline: Health workers run out of patience with Stormont budget delay
stories.claim: Northern Ireland hospital doctors will strike in November as the lack of a Stormont budget blocks a 3.5% pay award.
stories.summary: Northern Ireland's Executive has gone seven months into the financial year without a budget, blocking a recommended 3.5% pay rise for hospital doctors. Resident doctors plan a 24-hour walkout on 20 November, and consultants will run a reduced service the following Monday. The Royal College of Nursing has opened a ballot for industrial action. Finance Minister John O'Dowd says pressures are around £1.6bn against a £525m offer from the UK government. Secretary of State Chris Bryant has set January as the absolute deadline for a deal.
key_points: Resident doctors will hold a 24-hour walkout on Friday 20 November.
Consultants and specialists will operate a much-reduced service the following Monday.

The UK government has offered an extra £1.5bn over three years, with £525m in the first year.
Finance Minister John O'Dowd says departmental pressures are around £1.6bn.
The emergency budget money is expected to run out in January.
stories.story:
Hospital doctors in Northern Ireland have announced two strikes next month because the region still has no budget for the current financial year. The Executive is seven months into the year without one, and although day-to-day services and wages continue under emergency procedures, the absence of a budget means a 3.5% pay uplift recommended by an independent pay body and accepted by the health minister cannot be paid. Doctors elsewhere in the UK have received the increase since April.

The British Medical Association says the health minister told it there would be no pay rise before Christmas, if at all. Resident doctors will hold a 24-hour walkout on 20 November, and consultants and specialists will run a much-reduced service the following Monday. The Royal College of Nursing has also opened a ballot for industrial action over the same pay issue, arguing that nurses in Northern Ireland are repeatedly left waiting for awards given elsewhere in the UK.

The budget deadlock stems from a consensus among the Stormont parties that the UK's devolution funding formula leaves them too short of money to produce a workable plan. The UK government has accepted more funding is needed and offered £1.5bn over three years, with £525m this year. Finance Minister John O'Dowd says pressures this year are about £1.6bn and that public sector pay alone costs around £500m. Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant has criticised overspending and set January as the absolute deadline, when emergency money runs out. Analysts such as Ann Watt of Pivotal think tank see little room for a quick fix, so strikes may be hard to avoid.

stories.headline: Crypto audits give investors false sense of security as Q3 hacks cost $1.18 billion, Hacken says
stories.claim: Hacken reports crypto hacks cost $1.18bn in Q3, arguing audits miss the systems attackers actually target.
stories.summary: Blockchain security firm Hacken says hackers stole $1.18 billion across 107 incidents in the third quarter, up 55% on the previous quarter. Most of the losses, $906.8 million, came through compromised suppliers, developer tools or unpatched components outside audit scope. The largest single incident was the September attack on Bitget, which lost at least $352 million. Hacken argues investors place too much trust in audit badges that do not cover the full system.
key_points: Hacken counts $1.18bn of stolen crypto across 107 incidents in Q3, 55% more than in Q2.
About $906.8m of losses came from compromised suppliers, developer tools or unfixed components.
Bitget lost at least $352m in September after a third-party security product was exploited.
Ledger reported a hardware 'spy' implant in a device sold by a reseller, causing about $93m in losses.
More than $700m in assets at two venues relied on key arrangements Hacken considered inadequate.
Hacken says responsibility lies with firms holding customer funds to patch vulnerabilities promptly.
stories.story:
Crypto investors may be relying too heavily on security audits that do not cover the parts of systems hackers actually target, according to blockchain security firm Hacken. Its quarterly report found that hackers stole $1.18 billion across 107 incidents in the third quarter, a rise of 55% on the previous quarter. Of that total, $906.8 million came from compromised suppliers or developer tools, unpatched security fixes, or components left out of the latest review.

The largest single loss was the September attack on the exchange Bitget, which lost at least $352 million after hackers exploited a flaw in a third-party security product to reach its withdrawal systems. Hacken also cited a July exploit across several bridges and cross-chain protocols that lost more than $35 million in six hours, and a hardware wallet issue in which Ledger said an unauthorised implant was found in a device sold by a Southeast Asian reseller, causing losses of about $93 million.

Hacken's co-founder, Andrii Matiukhin, said the core problem is scope, as complete audits of every component are expensive and teams often audit only critical parts. He said that venues holding more than $700 million relied on signing arrangements or administrative keys that were not adequately secured, though he stressed that no live bug had been found in the reviewed venues. He also flagged slow fixes to known vulnerabilities, particularly where several blockchains use the same software.

Hacken concludes that the responsibility rests with the companies holding customer funds, which should track vulnerabilities and install fixes quickly rather than relying on an audit completed months or years earlier. The findings point to a continuing risk for the crypto sector, where large losses remain common despite growing security spending.
stories.market_take: Large hacks can dent sentiment toward crypto-linked equities, though the effect on listed firms is usually modest.

stories.story:
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, has called on the government to act in the Budget to help businesses employ more young people. Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, she referred to around one million young people who are not in employment, education or training, known as Neets. She said that unemployment among young people had risen by more than 174,000.

The article notes that youth unemployment reached an 11-year high in the middle of this year, and that the number of Neets passed one million before falling back. Whately linked the trend to rising diagnoses of mental health conditions, referring to an independent review published on 8 October by the Department of Health and Social Care. She argued that the welfare system discourages people from taking jobs or training, especially those claiming Personal Independence Payments.

Whately also said young people face repeated job rejections and that the jobs must exist in the first place, while still sending a strong message about expectations. Her remarks are political criticism of the Labour government's record. The article links them to earlier City AM reporting that the chancellor, John Healey, is drawing up measures to reduce the cost of hiring under-25s. Such a measure is expected to feature in his Budget statement on 28 October, according to sources cited by City AM. Any policy would need to be set out formally before its effect can be judged.

stories.story:
Two people died when a light aircraft came down near Loch Lomond in Scotland on Friday. The dead are an 80-year-old man, understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis, and a 16-year-old boy whose identity has not been released.

The Piper Tomahawk II had departed Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of Drymen near Stirling. Emergency services were called to the scene at around 16:45. The aircraft is registered to Leading Edge Flight Training in Renfrew.

Earlier that day the plane had flown from Cumbernauld Airport, then to Glasgow, on to Newport-on-Tay and back to Glasgow, before taking off on its final flight. Glasgow Airport's managing director described the event as deeply tragic.

The Air Accidents Investigation Branch is leading the inquiry, and temporary airspace restrictions remain over the area. A nearby road is closed and hillwalkers have been rerouted. Tributes from former students describe the instructor as an experienced aviator and a good friend. The cause of the crash has not been reported.

stories.story:
Israeli restrictions on the import of commercial goods into Gaza have entered their fifth consecutive day, causing prices of basic foods to climb quickly. Residents in Gaza City and northern areas say families are stockpiling what they can, while poorer households struggle to buy even small quantities.

According to a local trader's account reported by Al Jazeera, a carton of eggs has risen from 35 shekels to between 60 and 70 shekels, and onions and avocados have also become much dearer. A displaced woman in Beit Lahiya said a sack of flour had risen from roughly 25–35 shekels to about 80 shekels, and that her family now relies mainly on rice and lentils.

Israel said the suspension followed a dispute over fees involving Palestinian merchants and Hamas, which still has some authority in Gaza. Gaza's Government Media Office rejected that explanation, saying no taxes or government fees had been imposed on commercial trucks. It said a 10,000-shekel figure cited by Israel related to a voluntary community fund, and that a 30 percent rate for cash transactions had been agreed with the Chamber of Commerce to deal with cash shortages.

The UN's humanitarian office, OCHA, reported that food prices in Gaza in September 2026 averaged 204 percent above pre-October 2023 levels. The Gaza office warned that continued restrictions would deepen the humanitarian and economic crisis. The article does not indicate when the crossings will reopen, and residents fear the closure could last for weeks.

stories.claim: Some conservative US states, including Missouri and Iowa, are not taking up a Medicaid hardship exemption for new work requirements.
stories.summary: Several conservative US states, including Missouri and Iowa, are declining a federal hardship exemption under new Medicaid work requirements. According to research from the KFF health policy nonprofit, these states have counties that would qualify. Experts cite ideological opposition and administrative burden as possible reasons. The new rules, starting 1 January, require certain adults to work or take part in qualifying activities for 80 hours a month. Critics warn that many people could lose coverage.
key_points: Missouri and Iowa are not using a federal hardship exemption despite having qualifying counties, per KFF research.
New York City adopted the high-unemployment exemption for the Bronx, covering about 200,000 residents.
Federal Medicaid work requirements take effect on 1 January and require 80 hours a month of qualifying activity.
Experts suggest political ideology and administrative burden may explain the decisions.
Arkansas's 2018 work requirements led to more than 18,000 people losing coverage, with no clear rise in employment.
stories.story:
Some conservative US states are choosing not to use a federal hardship exemption linked to the new Medicaid work requirements. Research from the healthcare policy nonprofit KFF found that states including Missouri and Iowa have counties that would qualify for the exemption but are not planning to apply it. The Guardian has asked both state departments for comment.

The new federal requirements, due to start on 1 January, mean adults enrolled through the Affordable Care Act Medicaid expansion must work, study, volunteer or do another qualifying activity for at least 80 hours a month. The law also includes exemptions for people who are hospitalised, need to travel for care, or live in areas hit by disasters or high unemployment. New York City has adopted the high-unemployment exemption for the Bronx, where about 200,000 residents would otherwise be affected.

Experts quoted in the report suggest political views and administrative workload may explain the states' choices. One KFF official said supporters of work requirements may feel they should apply evenly across all areas, while another point raised was the effort needed to keep eligibility systems updated. Academics and advocates warn that the requirements could lead to significant coverage losses. They point to Arkansas, where more than 18,000 people lost coverage in 2018 without a clear increase in employment.

stories.story:
Bus company McGill's has strongly criticised the Scottish government's plans to bring bus services under public control. Sandy Easdale, who owns the firm with his brother James, said First Minister John Swinney had turned into a leader comparable to Idi Amin or Robert Mugabe, and accused both of bankrupting their countries. The remarks were reported by BBC Scotland.

The firm's chairman, Ralph Roberts, told BBC Scotland that the company had invested in local services and that the owners were angered by what they see as an attempt to confiscate their business. He said there had been a lack of dialogue, that alternative proposals had been ignored, and that the plans could cost taxpayers hundreds of millions of pounds a year. He also warned that McGill's would be competing for council contracts and could fail if it lost them, and that it was prepared to take legal action.

Swinney announced at the SNP conference in Aberdeen that buses would be brought under public control by 2031 through franchising and regulation, with a Bill to be tabled in Holyrood next year. The changes would give regional transport partnerships more control over routes and fares without the government directly owning the network. Swinney also extended the £2 bus fare cap to Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire from April, with plans to cover the whole country by the end of the parliamentary term in 2031.

Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth responded that the government was protecting the public after a series of route closures and described the current private model as a legacy of Thatcher-era deregulation. She said the government works with operators, and she noted that the Easdale brothers were significant donors to the Labour Party. The dispute highlights the tension between operators and public authorities over the future of bus provision in Scotland.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; the plans mainly affect private bus operators in Scotland.

stories.headline: France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
stories.claim: Raphael Glucksmann won the Socialist presidential primary in France, setting up a difficult bid for 2027 with youth voters leaning to Mélenchon.
stories.summary: Raphael Glucksmann won France's Socialist presidential primary on October 11 with 66% in the first round and will be the party's candidate for the 2027 election. He was flour-bombed after his victory speech. Polling puts him at about 10-11%, well behind far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon on 18%, and Mélenchon dominates among under-25s. Glucksmann's stance against working with the far left is central to his challenge.
key_points: Glucksmann won the Socialist primary with 66% of the vote in the first round on October 11.
A Toluna Harris Interactive poll projects him at 10-11%, against 18% for Mélenchon, though it was taken before his win.
In an Ipsos survey in September, Mélenchon scored 41% among under-25s, while Marine Le Pen had 20%.
Glucksmann rejects cooperation with La France Insoumise, a stance that sets him apart from party leader Olivier Faure.
He proposes reducing the CSG social tax on earned income and raising taxes on inheritances above €2 million.
Analysts say his core challenge is winning over left-wing voters who are young, financially stretched and loyal to Mélenchon.
stories.story:
Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for the centre-left Socialists, won the party's presidential primary in the first round on October 11, taking a clear 66% of the vote. He will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election. Shortly after leaving a restaurant in Paris's Belleville district, where he celebrated, he was hit by a flour bomb from an unidentified attacker. He then urged the left-wing populist Jean-Luc Mélenchon to condemn attacks by his supporters, although it was unclear whether the attacker was linked to Mélenchon's movement.

The main dividing question of the primary was whether the Socialists should cooperate with Mélenchon's La France Insoumise. Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left, while party leader Olivier Faure left the door open. Rivals questioned his experience, and former presidential candidate Ségolène Royal compared him to an intern seeking to run a company. A poll published the day after his win projected him at 10-11%, behind Mélenchon on 18%, though it was conducted before the primary result. Even so, that would be a clear improvement on the Socialists' 1.75% in 2022.

The article also highlights weaknesses in his position. Glucksmann is not a member of the Socialist Party, belonging instead to the small centre-left party Place Publique. Young voters are a particular problem: Mélenchon was at 41% among under-25s in a September Ipsos survey. Analyst Antoine Bristielle found that many loyal LFI supporters are young, educated city dwellers under financial pressure, while a group of roughly a third of left-wing voters, nearly half under 35, might consider backing the Socialists, Greens or LFI. Glucksmann's policies combine tax changes with strong support for Ukraine and European integration, which could also appeal to some centrist voters.

What happens next depends on whether the primary bounce translates into support in polls over the coming weeks, and whether Glucksmann can win over Mélenchon's voters without working with him. Mélenchon, meanwhile, is backing student protests and calls to lower the voting age to 16 and abolish the Parcoursup admissions system.

He said he would gradually return to his duties and thanked medical staff at Rome's Gemelli hospital. His surgeon says he is expected to recover fully in about 10 days and that there are no clinical reasons his November trip to South America should not go ahead.

The surgery confirmed adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

stories.story:
Pope Leo XIV greeted crowds in St Peter's Square on Sunday, 18 October, during the traditional Angelus blessing. It was his first public appearance since returning from hospital the previous day, where he had surgery to remove a malignant lung tumour. A week earlier, he had announced from the same window that a nodule had been found on his lung and would be removed.

In his remarks, he said that he would gradually resume his activities with God's help and the prayers of the faithful. He said the experience had made him feel closer to people facing illness, and thanked the doctors and nurses at Gemelli hospital. Visitors from Africa and the United States were among those who cheered. He told a reporter he was feeling 'much better' as he left hospital, after a shorter stay than expected.

The 71-year-old pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday. Surgery confirmed adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. This is the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. Histological testing of the tumour and nearby lymph nodes is still underway, and the results will guide whether he needs further treatment, which could include chemotherapy, a combination with immunotherapy or targeted oral medication.

His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, said the pope was expected to recover fully in around ten days and that there were no clinical reasons why his next major trip, from 6 to 17 November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, should not go ahead. The trip includes many flights and two helicopter journeys to high altitude. What happens next will depend on the test results and his recovery over the coming weeks.

stories.claim: An internal NHS England impact assessment says new single-sex ward guidance could bring delays and discrimination risks for trans patients.
stories.summary: An internal NHS England impact assessment, seen by the Guardian, finds that new guidance requiring trans people to use single-sex wards by biological sex could cause delays, greater risk of corridor care and discrimination. The guidance was published on Thursday and follows a 2025 Supreme Court ruling on the meaning of sex in the Equality Act. The assessment also identifies benefits for women, religious groups and some ethnic minorities, and suggests mitigations such as prioritising clinical need.
key_points: NHS England published guidance on Thursday that single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms should be used by biological sex.
The internal impact assessment flags possible delays, corridor care and worse health outcomes for trans people.
It warns trans people may avoid healthcare altogether if they face discrimination.
The document also identifies positive impacts for privacy, dignity and safety, and for some religious and minority-ethnic groups.
The guidance follows a 2025 Supreme Court ruling and an updated EHRC code of practice.
The assessment suggests case-by-case decisions and says the policy does not apply in A&E or intensive care.
stories.story:
The Guardian has seen an internal NHS England impact assessment which concludes that new guidance on single-sex spaces could have a number of negative effects on trans people. Under the guidance, published on Thursday, single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms should be used according to a person's biological sex rather than their gender identity. Trans people are to be accommodated in line with their biological sex while their clinical needs are met and their privacy, dignity and safety are protected.

The assessment, which looked at all protected characteristics, found that the policy could bring delays and a greater risk of corridor care for trans people if side rooms were not available, with possible harm to physical and mental health. It also said trans people could fear being outed and could face discrimination, and that they might be pushed into wards matching their birth sex. The document warned that the policy could create division between cisgender and transgender people, and that some women who do not present in line with social expectations could be questioned about their sex.

The assessment also found benefits. It said the policy's focus on privacy, dignity and safety for men and women, and greater legal accuracy, would be positive, as would effects for pregnant or breastfeeding women, some religious groups and some minority-ethnic communities. The guidance follows a 2025 Supreme Court ruling that the terms 'woman' and 'sex' in the Equality Act refer to biological sex. An updated code of practice from the Equality and Human Rights Commission says the rules must be applied on the basis of biological sex and acknowledges that trans people are likely to be disadvantaged by them.

The assessment suggests that negative effects could be reduced by prioritising clinical need and making decisions on a case-by-case basis. It notes that the policy does not apply in A&E or intensive care units. The story is an exclusive based on a document seen by the Guardian, so the wider reaction and how the NHS will respond to these findings are not yet clear.

stories.story:

Regional governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being put out. The attack also struck a logistics centre belonging to the e-commerce firm Ozon and a regional data centre of the social network VK. Twelve apartment buildings and two homes were damaged, Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed, and mobile internet disruption was possible. Kyiv had not commented at the time of reporting.

The attack comes after a short-lived pause. Ukraine had stopped striking Russian oil facilities for three days after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire last week. Ukraine says Russia continued attacks on its energy sector, and Zelensky said Russia had targeted it 76 times since the ceasefire was announced. Ukraine then resumed its strikes earlier this week, which drew criticism from Trump. Russia's defence ministry said it had downed over 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight into Sunday.

The wider context includes a US deal to import Russian diesel, intended to lower US fuel prices that have risen during the Iran conflict ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky has said the deal amounts to the US investing in Russia's war effort, and Trump's decision to suspend some sanctions on Russia has drawn criticism, including from some Republicans. Both sides have been hitting each other's energy infrastructure ahead of winter, and the UN said the first two weeks of October were the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.

Russian strikes have left hundreds of thousands without power, and Zelensky said tens of thousands were still without electricity. The attack coincided with the opening of Putin's flagship economic forum. Earlier this month Ukraine also attacked Yandex, causing disruption. Whether the energy truce holds, and how Moscow responds, remains to be seen.

stories.headline: EPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compounds
stories.claim: The EPA quietly changed its website wording after admitting Pfoa and Pfos are still produced in the US, while Inhance continues making containers.
stories.summary: The US Environmental Protection Agency has quietly altered website wording that said Pfoa and Pfos had been phased out in the United States. The change followed a complaint from the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (Peer). The agency's own revised text now acknowledges that quantities of Pfoa may still be produced, imported and used, and that Pfos has limited ongoing uses. Houston-based Inhance continues to make plastic containers that have been found to leach Pfoa, and the company denies measurable leaching. The story highlights ongoing tension over PFAS regulation.

The updated text acknowledges that Pfoa may still be produced, imported and used in the US.

stories.story:
The Guardian reports that the Environmental Protection Agency has quietly revised wording on its website that had said two harmful PFAS compounds, Pfoa and Pfos, had been phased out in the United States. The change was made last month after a complaint from Peer, a non-profit that works on environmental science policy. The updated website now says quantities of Pfoa may be produced, imported and used, and notes that Pfos is still produced in the US for some limited uses. An EPA official wrote in a September response that the agency was updating its websites at Peer's request.

The report focuses on Houston-based Inhance, which makes plastic containers that the EPA and Peer say can release Pfoa into their contents. The company says the chemical is present only as an impurity, that there is no measurable leaching, and that it has reduced Pfoa impurity levels by 90%. The EPA has issued orders against the company in recent years, including a 2022 order to cease production and a 2023 order that was later overturned by a federal appeals court. A lawsuit brought by Peer was dismissed after a judge ruled the group lacked standing.

Background to the story goes back to a 2015 EPA agreement with eight PFAS producers to phase out Pfoa and Pfos, which was widely presented as major progress, though it stopped short of a ban. Public health experts cite the International Agency for Research on Cancer, which classes Pfoa as carcinogenic to humans. Critics, including Peer's science policy director, argue the phase-out was inadequate and that the EPA should introduce outright bans and enforcement.

The EPA did not immediately comment on the report. The matter is likely to keep drawing scrutiny over whether federal agencies are accurately describing PFAS use and whether enforcement against producers is adequate.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect, though stricter PFAS rules could affect chemical and container makers.

stories.claim: A kerosene leak has spread along almost 2.5 miles of the River Taff in South Wales, prompting health advice to residents.
stories.summary: Natural Resources Wales says a kerosene spill has spread along almost 2.5 miles of the River Taff near Cardiff, affecting communities including Nantgarw, Treforest and Taff's Well. Residents have been advised to keep windows and doors closed and avoid contact with the water. Up to 25,000 litres of kerosene is reported to have entered the river. The leak came from an underground surface water drainage system, and its source has not been named. Officials say the amount of fuel entering the river has fallen, but cleanup and environmental testing are ongoing.
key_points: Kerosene has spread along almost 2.5 miles of the River Taff, according to Natural Resources Wales.
Up to 25,000 litres of kerosene is reported to have entered the river.

stories.story:
Natural Resources Wales (NRW) has said a kerosene leak has spread along almost 2.5 miles (4km) of the River Taff in South Wales. Reports of pollution first came in on Saturday morning, when the spill was described as affecting about one mile of the river. The affected places include Nantgarw, Treforest, Taff's Well, Tongwynlais and other villages. NRW says it found the source at 19:30 BST on Friday, but it has not named the source at this stage and is working to establish how the fuel entered the drainage system.

NRW says the pollution was discharging from an underground surface water drainage system and that the amount of fuel has fallen significantly. South Wales Fire and Rescue Service has helped install specialist equipment to collect fuel, and absorbent materials have been used to contain it. Water samples are being taken to assess the environmental damage. Public Health Wales has advised people living nearby to keep windows and doors closed, avoid contact with the water and call NHS 111 if they feel unwell. Residents reported strong fuel smells and eye irritation, and one said that up to 25,000 litres had entered the river, a figure NRW has given to residents.

Local residents and a former hazardous materials officer describe serious effects on the community, including dead fish and a loss of wildlife in places. The former officer said recovery could take years and that kerosene does not mix with water, so it could keep polluting. Kerosene is a fuel that floats on water, which can make clean-up harder.

The next steps include continued investigation to stop the leak completely, further sampling to measure the environmental impact, and work to clear the drainage system. Residents and local officials will be waiting for the source to be named and for a full assessment of the damage to the river.

stories.headline: 'Like we had a war': France left reeling after nationwide violent protests
stories.claim: Nationwide protests in France turned violent, with about 1,800 arrests, damaged businesses and a burnt Limoges town hall.
stories.summary: Protests across France on Saturday over the cost of living and school conditions turned violent, with about 1,800 arrests according to the Interior Minister. Around 1,500 businesses were damaged, with losses estimated in the hundreds of millions of euros, and the 19th-century town hall in Limoges was largely destroyed by fire. The interior ministry put attendance at 550,000, while the CGT union said 800,000 took part. Political figures have traded blame ahead of presidential elections in about six months. The government is due to hold a crisis meeting on Monday.
key_points: Around 1,800 people were arrested across France, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

stories.story:
France was dealing with the aftermath of nationwide protests on Saturday that turned violent in several cities. The interior ministry said 550,000 people attended, while the CGT union put the figure at 800,000. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said about 1,800 people were arrested over the protests and looting. Around 1,500 businesses were damaged, and losses are estimated in the hundreds of millions of euros, according to the Retail and Trade Federation. Hundreds of shops were looted in Paris and other cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg.

The historic town hall of Limoges was largely destroyed by a fire that the local prefect said had been set deliberately. Other buildings, including a tourist office in Lyon, were also set alight. Around 500 police, firefighters and paramedics were reported hurt. A 17-year-old lost a hand after a crowd-control grenade in Saint-Étienne. A death during the main Paris march was said by officials to be health-related and not linked to the violence.

The protests began as anger over school conditions, including teacher shortages and poor buildings, and grew into a wider movement that drew in trade unions and supporters of the yellow vest movement. The main grievance is the cost of living, which has been pushed up partly by the war in the Middle East. The government's proposed 2027 budget includes a 54 billion euro package of spending cuts and tax measures, and the protests coincided with a public sector strike.

Political reactions have been sharp. The government and Marine Le Pen blamed ultra-left groups, while Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused authorities of inflaming tensions. US Vice President JD Vance made a remark on X suggesting the unrest was linked to immigration. Lecornu is due to chair a crisis meeting on Monday covering insurance and aid for shops and the prosecution of those responsible. President Emmanuel Macron, who is in his final months before elections, has said those responsible would be prosecuted and punished.
stories.market_take: Ongoing unrest and the 2027 budget dispute could weigh on French assets and retail sector sentiment.

stories.headline: 10 million Americans are using advance loan apps to get their paychecks in advance—and it’s costing them hundreds of dollars more, report finds
stories.claim: A Center for Responsible Lending report finds earned wage access apps cost users hundreds of dollars a year in fees and tips.
stories.summary: A report from the Center for Responsible Lending's Julian Bond Institute, based on bank transactions from 10,000 consumers, finds that over 10 million Americans used earned wage access or on-demand pay apps as of 2024. The analysis found 96% of direct-to-consumer payday-style advances included fees or tips, averaging about $208 a year. Economists and consumer advocates warn of loan stacking and hidden debt, and the CFPB withdrew a proposed disclosure rule in December 2025.
key_points: As of 2024, more than 10 million Americans used earned wage access or on-demand pay tools.
An analysis of bank transactions from 10,000 consumers found 96% of direct-to-consumer payday-style advances carried fees or tips.
Fees and tips average about $208 a year, or roughly $17 a month, per user.
The report estimates an average APR of around 232% for these advances.
The CFPB withdrew a 2024 proposal in December 2025 that would have treated fees and tips as finance charges.
Researchers warn that loan stacking across apps could raise delinquency risk and pass costs on to shoppers through higher prices.
stories.story:
A new report from the Center for Responsible Lending's Julian Bond Institute says a growing number of Americans are using apps that let workers draw on their pay before payday, and that these tools are proving costly. The analysis looked at bank transactions from 10,000 consumers and found that 96% of direct-to-consumer versions of payday-style loans included fees or optional tips. On average these charges came to nearly $208 a year, or about $17 a month.

According to the piece, more than 10 million Americans used some form of earned wage access or on-demand pay as of 2024. These tools are mostly used by people earning under $50,000, with food and rent cited as the main reasons for borrowing. The apps usually do not run credit checks or charge interest, but fees for fast transfers, membership charges and tips can push the effective annual rate to around 232%, close to traditional payday lenders.

The article places this in the wider context of short-term finance growing since the pandemic. It cites Datos Insights data showing transaction volume on on-demand pay apps tripling between 2018 and 2020, and LendingTree data showing nearly a third of Americans have used buy-now, pay-later to buy groceries. Experts quoted are concerned about loan stacking, where people take several small loans from different apps, which can be hard for other lenders to see and can raise the risk of missed payments.

Regulation has moved the other way. In 2024 the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau proposed requiring fees and tips to be disclosed as finance charges, but in December 2025 the agency under Russell Vought withdrew that proposal, ruling that fees and voluntary tips were not finance charges. One economist's model suggests retailers raise prices to cover merchant fees from buy-now, pay-later providers, meaning the cost could fall on all shoppers. The article does not describe any new policy response.
stories.market_take: Possible longer-term pressure on fintech lenders and BNPL providers if regulation tightens, though no immediate market move is indicated.

stories.story:
A cross-party group of MPs on the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has called on the Competition and Markets Authority to launch a full market investigation into the UK live music industry. The committee said on 18 October that it was 'pressing' the regulator to act before the end of the year, and it repeated a call first made in a May report. Its particular concern is the dominance of Live Nation, the owner of ticketing platform Ticketmaster.

The committee cites figures showing that Live Nation directly controlled 58% of the 23.1 million primary tickets on sale in 2025, rising to 66% when sales by affiliated companies are included. The MPs say these figures raised 'red flags' against all three of the CMA's factors for assessing market dominance. Concerns were raised with the watchdog after ticket sales for the Oasis reunion tour, where some tickets were sold for thousands of pounds. Liam Byrne MP, the committee chair, said the industry should reward talent rather than market power and that the committee had found a climate of fear for artists and grassroots venues.

The CMA responded that it is giving active and careful consideration to undertaking markets work in this area, but it has not yet announced a full investigation. The committee says it is writing to the regulator to ask for details and a timeline of its next steps. Any formal investigation would be a lengthy process, and its outcome is uncertain. stories.headline: I fear a Budget tax raid on pensioners, but the Chancellor should leave well alone: JEFF PRESTRIDGE
stories.claim: Pre-Budget speculation suggests pensioners could face higher taxes, including a 'two up, two down' income tax and NI switch.
stories.summary: A personal finance columnist writes that Budget rumours are quieter than before, but warns that pensioners could face a tax raid. He points to a Resolution Foundation proposal for a 'two up, two down' tax switch, which would raise income tax and cut employee National Insurance. He also notes that the Financial Times reports Chancellor John Healey has rejected aligning capital gains tax with income tax rates. The piece is opinion, and the proposals are think-tank ideas rather than government plans.
key_points: The columnist says pre-Budget rumours are subdued compared with the previous two Budgets under Rachel Reeves.
The Resolution Foundation proposes a 'two up, two down' tax switch, adding 2p to income tax and cutting employee NI by the same amount.
AJ Bell estimates a pensioner with £35,000 retirement income would pay almost £450 more under the proposal.
The FT reports Healey has rejected aligning CGT rates with income tax rates.
The Budget is due on 28 October and the Chancellor has not confirmed any of these measures.
stories.story:
A personal finance columnist writes that the usual rumour mill ahead of the Budget has been quieter this time than it was before the previous two Budgets, when speculation about cuts to tax-free pension cash had prompted many people to withdraw money. He suggests this could reflect Chancellor John Healey's reluctance to raise taxes during a cost-of-living squeeze, or a tighter grip on Treasury leaks. He also warns that the quiet may not last, and that more detail could emerge in the days ahead.

The main pre-Budget idea discussed is from the Resolution Foundation, a think-tank, which has proposed about £8bn of tax rises to pay for support for struggling households and higher defence spending. Its suggested 'two up, two down' change would raise income tax by 2p in the pound and cut employee National Insurance by the same amount. Because pensioners do not pay NI, they would face higher bills, and AJ Bell estimates that someone with £35,000 of retirement income would pay just under £450 more. A worker on a £35,000 salary would see no change in take-home pay. The Resolution Foundation itself accepts the idea would be controversial.

The columnist also notes the only near-certainty so far is that capital gains tax and income tax rates will not be aligned, according to the FT, which says Healey rejected that idea. Current CGT rates are 18% for basic rate taxpayers and 24% for higher and additional rate taxpayers, above a £3,000 annual exemption. The columnist points out that CGT rates could still be nudged up, and that past increases have taken effect immediately. He argues that pensioners should be spared, and that the proposal would also conflict with Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to raise NI, income tax or VAT, although the pledge is open to interpretation on pensioners.

The Budget is scheduled for 28 October, and the government has not confirmed any of these measures. Readers should treat the proposals as think-tank suggestions and commentary rather than policy.

stories.headline: The next ayahuasca? Gabon fights to protect sacred plant from US drug companies
stories.claim: Gabon is seeking to protect the sacred iboga plant as US interest in ibogaine for addiction treatment grows.
stories.summary: A Guardian Business feature reports on Gabon's efforts to protect iboga, a root bark central to Bwiti ritual traditions, as foreign pharmaceutical interest in its alkaloid ibogaine rises. A US executive order signed in April named ibogaine and directed federal agencies to create a treatment pathway. Researchers and practitioners warn that commercial harvesting, which can kill the shrub, threatens the species, and that scientific study of wild populations is underfunded.
key_points: A US executive order signed on 18 April named ibogaine and directed federal agencies to build a treatment pathway.
Ibogaine is being studied for addiction treatment, but early studies are small and uncontrolled.
Commercial extraction that removes whole root systems kills the iboga shrub and threatens wild stocks.
Lee White, a former Gabonese environment minister, reports severe local over-harvesting and a lack of funding for research.
stories.story:
The Guardian reports on the cultural and ecological stakes around iboga, a slow-growing rainforest shrub from central Africa whose root bark has long been used in Gabonese ritual traditions, particularly within the Bwiti spiritual practice. Demand is now rising from abroad because pharmaceutical companies see potential in ibogaine, a compound derived from the plant, as a treatment for addiction. A US executive order signed on 18 April named ibogaine compounds and directed federal agencies to create a treatment pathway for eligible patients, and Texas has granted $50m for a multicentre trial.

The evidence for ibogaine remains limited. A 2024 study of 30 US special operations veterans reported large falls in PTSD, depression and anxiety scores a month after treatment, but the study was small, uncontrolled and included other therapies, so it could not establish efficacy. Commercial treatment is already on offer; one clinic in Cancún lists programmes costing between $13,500 and $19,500.

The article's central concern is ecological. Small amounts of root bark can be harvested without killing the plant, but commercial collectors sometimes remove whole root systems, which kills the shrub. A 2012 report documented this practice, and a conservation group has worked with communities on cultivation since 2015. Lee White, who led Gabon's national parks agency, described wild iboga as rare and poorly studied and said his teams found severe over-harvesting in several areas. He said he could not secure funding for a study of its distribution and genetic variation.

Practitioners in Gabon, including temple leaders, say that iboga is only one element of a wider spiritual practice and that the plant should be considered within its whole ecosystem. Some say researchers have taken their remedies without sharing benefits. The piece suggests that without better funding and protections, the species could be lost before its medical potential is properly understood.
stories.market_take: Interest in ibogaine could benefit listed drug developers working on addiction treatments, but the sector impact is speculative and limited for now.

Other points in the piece include positioning data. Funding rates are at or below zero and leverage has been largely cleared, which some see as leaving room for a short-covering squeeze. stories.headline: Researchers train AI to detect concealed handguns using Wi-Fi signals
stories.claim: Swedish Defence Research Agency researchers built WiFireNet, an experimental AI that spots concealed handguns from Wi-Fi signal distortion.
stories.summary: Researchers at the Swedish Defence Research Agency (FOI) have developed WiFireNet, an experimental AI system that attempts to detect concealed handguns using Wi-Fi signals rather than cameras or metal detectors. The method analyses channel state information, the way an object alters ambient Wi-Fi as it passes through or reflects signals. In controlled indoor trials the system reached an average handgun-detection precision of 72.5%, falling to 53.8% under stricter location requirements. The team has released its code, models and dataset as open source, while privacy critics warn about the lack of regulation for Wi-Fi sensing.
key_points: FOI researchers posted a paper on arXiv describing WiFireNet, a system that detects concealed handguns from Wi-Fi signal data.
The system uses a transmitter, a receiver and a deep learning model that reads channel state information.
Average handgun-detection precision was 72.5% in trials with up to four moving people, but fell to 53.8% when exact weapon location was required.
Performance drops in unfamiliar indoor layouts, and the prototype used the 1999 802.11a standard.
Future phases plan to use Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 with higher-resolution data.
Critics warn that Wi-Fi sensing raises privacy concerns in the absence of regulatory frameworks.
stories.story:
Researchers at the Swedish Defence Research Agency (FOI) have described an experimental artificial intelligence system that aims to identify concealed handguns by analysing how people and objects disturb ordinary Wi-Fi signals. The work was detailed in a paper posted on arXiv on 13 October. The system, named WiFireNet, is positioned as a non-intrusive alternative to visible cameras and metal detectors, which the researchers describe as either conspicuous or cumbersome.

The approach relies on channel state information, the data describing how an object changes Wi-Fi signals through reflection and penetration depending on its shape, orientation and material. To train the model, the team built a dataset called the WiFire Dataset by recording video of people walking with objects, from phones to handguns, while simultaneously capturing Wi-Fi signals. They included a plastic handgun, a metal water bottle, a real metal handgun and a phone so the system could tell a gun apart from similar everyday items.

In controlled trials with up to four moving people in a small indoor space, the system reached an average handgun-detection precision of 72.5%. When the task required pinpointing the weapon's exact position on a person, precision dropped to 53.8%. The neural network also struggled in unfamiliar indoor layouts that it had not been tested on. The researchers stress that the system is still experimental and the prototype used an old wireless standard to prove the concept.

The team has made the code, models and dataset open source to encourage further work, and plans to move to modern Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 networks with richer data. The article notes that Wi-Fi sensing is becoming more popular as a surveillance technique because it needs little specialised equipment. Critics argue that its spread, together with the absence of regulatory frameworks, raises serious privacy concerns. The results suggest the technology is far from ready for real-world security use, though it marks a notable research step.

sources.title: Researchers train AI to detect concealed handguns using Wi-Fi signals

key_points: The Dock 4 swaps drone batteries in about 25 seconds, with a turnaround of under 45 seconds from landing to takeoff.
Each battery pack is rated at 260 Wh and can be charged from 15% to 95% in roughly 27 minutes.

stories.story:
DJI, the Chinese drone maker, has launched the Dock 4, a battery-swapping drone dock that it says is its first product of this kind. According to a company press release, the dock replaces a drone's battery automatically in about 25 seconds, so the aircraft can take off again within 45 seconds of landing. Without battery swapping, a normal recharge would take around 30 minutes. DJI markets the product for emergency response, calling it a dock-as-a-first-responder solution.

The dock can charge two battery packs at once, each rated at 260 Wh, and estimates say each can be charged from 15% to 95% in about 27 minutes. The packs can also provide backup power for the dock, and with at least two packs loaded the dock can keep swapping batteries during a grid power cut. The dock weighs 66 kg without accessories. It works only with the new Matrice 5TD drone, which carries three 50 MP cameras, thermal sensors, LiDAR, radar and a laser rangefinder, and it can detect 17 types of object.

The kit is available to order from DJI partners in China at 167,999 yuan, roughly $25,000 for the hardware alone. However, the product is not FCC-authorised and cannot be sold in the United States. In December last year the FCC added all foreign-made drones and their critical components to its Covered List, which blocks new models from authorisation unless a US agency certifies they pose no security risk. DJI has sued the commission this year. A separate FCC proposal from August could also remove previously authorised foreign drones with LiDAR or thermal sensors from sale, though no final order had been issued as of 17 October.

The launch underlines how DJI is pushing into automated drone operations for public safety while its US access is restricted. Whether the dock gains a meaningful foothold will depend on how the regulatory dispute develops and on demand from customers outside the US.
stories.market_take: Limited direct effect on listed companies, though US restrictions on DJI's products remain a background risk for drone supply chains.

Licence plate readers are widely used by police and cities, which say they help track suspected criminals and improve public safety. Police departments previously objected when Waze added a feature in 2015 that let users report officers' locations, so there may be pushback against MapQuest's move as well. stories.story:
Business Insider has launched a new series called The AI Data Grab, which examines how AI companies are now seeking data on how humans actually work, having already scraped much of the public web. Three articles published in the same week illustrate the trend. The first, reported by Charles Rollet, Tom Carter and Stephen Council, describes a growing market in which AI firms offer businesses substantial sums for anonymised workplace records, including Slack messages, emails, presentations and internal documents.

The purpose of this material is to teach AI systems how people solve problems, collaborate, make decisions and carry out long, multi-step tasks. Such workflows are seen as the foundation for the next generation of AI agents. The reporting says the prices involved reach six and even seven figures for some businesses, which indicates how valuable this kind of data has become.

A second piece, by Melia Robinson, looks at law firms that are building their own AI systems based on decades of legal expertise. Rather than relying only on off-the-shelf tools, these firms aim to turn their accumulated knowledge into a competitive advantage. A third story, by Rya Jetha, reports that AI companies pay people to film themselves doing real-world jobs, such as cooking dinners or packing warehouses, so that robots can learn everyday physical tasks.

Taken together, the pieces suggest a shift in how AI is developed. The first wave of generative AI focused on larger models and faster chips, whereas the next stage is about machines learning how work gets done. The series raises questions about how workplace data is collected and used, though the excerpt provided does not cover privacy or consent in detail. It is a useful overview of a growing market for training data.

stories.headline: Typo-squatting attacks with major domains are still viable
stories.claim: Researchers show that a Cyrillic-based lookalike of apple.com can evade Chromium's typosquatting protections.
stories.summary: A Tom's Hardware article, based on research from Have I Been Squatted, shows that the domain 'аррӏө.com' can pass Chromium's anti-spoofing checks despite imitating apple.com. The trick relies on a Cyrillic character, ө, which is not on Chromium's list of 29 confusable Cyrillic characters. The article explains how Chromium's rules work and where they fall short. It concludes that companies should register lookalike domains and encourage passkeys, which are bound to specific domains.
key_points: The domain аррӏө.com evades Chromium's protections because the character ө is not on its list of 29 confusable Cyrillic characters.
Chromium shows Punycode for mixed-alphabet lookalikes and blocks all-Cyrillic lookalikes from the list.
A 2020 study found Chromium caught 64.1% of lookalike attempts, ahead of Firefox and Safari.
Chromium checks over 8,000 popular domains, with stronger checks on 836 of them.
Researchers recommend registering lookalike domains and using passkeys, which only work on their registered domain.
stories.story:
Tom's Hardware reports on research by Have I Been Squatted, which shows that typosquatting attacks using internationalised domain names remain viable. The researchers used the domain аррӏө.com, which looks like apple.com but is not identical to it, to show that a specific combination of Cyrillic characters can slip past several layers of protection in Chromium-based browsers.

The weakness is subtle. Chromium blocks domains that mix alphabets, displaying them in Punycode instead, and it also keeps a list of 29 Cyrillic characters that closely resemble Latin letters. Using only those characters is blocked. The character ө, however, is not on that list, which lets the test domain pass. The article notes that a future Chromium release could close the gap.

The piece places the issue in the wider history of internationalised domain names, which the IETF allowed in order to support non-Latin scripts. Those same scripts contain many visually similar characters, which makes detection hard. A 2020 study cited in the article found Chromium caught 64.1% of lookalike attempts, with Firefox and Safari behind it. Chromium underpins Chrome, Edge and Brave.

The researchers advise companies worried about impersonation to register lookalike domains and to encourage passkey use, since passkeys are tied to a specific domain and will not work on a fake site. The article suggests that no rule set can fully solve the problem, so defence will remain a matter of layered measures.

stories.claim: Joining Ethernet cables with couplers can cause problems, so a single longer cable or a switch is usually better.
stories.summary: Engadget advises against joining two Ethernet cables with a coupler for permanent setups, since the extra connection can cause dropouts or drop speeds. A single longer cable is simpler, and a network switch is better when more wired ports are needed. The article cites trueCABLE tests showing that four couplers failed while three generally passed. It also notes the 100-metre copper length limit, which a coupler cannot extend.
key_points: A coupler is simply two RJ45 sockets joined together and does not boost signal.
Each extra join is a potential failure point, causing dropouts or falling back to 100 Mbps.
The standard copper Ethernet channel limit is 100 metres (328 feet), including patch cords.
trueCABLE tests found configurations with four couplers failed, while three generally passed.
An unmanaged five-port Gigabit switch can cost around $15 and needs no configuration.
stories.story:
Engadget offers practical advice for anyone whose Ethernet cable has become too short after moving a desk or equipment. A small RJ45 coupler can join two cables together without needing power or configuration, and a good-quality coupler should not noticeably slow a connection. However, the article argues that the coupler adds a connection that can fail, particularly if it is cheap or easily knocked.

Symptoms of a poor join can include occasional dropouts, transmission errors, or a link that falls back from 1 Gbps to 100 Mbps. The advice is to test with a good cable without the coupler before troubleshooting the router or contacting an internet provider. A coupler also does not extend the length limit, which is 100 metres for copper Ethernet including patch cords.

The article cites testing by trueCABLE using a Fluke DSX-8000 tester on Cat6 and Cat6A cables. Configurations with three couplers generally passed, one only marginally, while those with four failed. The results depend on the specific parts used, but they suggest that adding joins unnecessarily is a poor idea.

For a permanent setup, the recommendation is a single cable of the right length, routed with some slack. Where a cable already runs to a room with several devices, a small unmanaged switch is the better choice, since each port creates a separate link with its own distance limit. Anyone installing a camera or wireless access point should also check for Power over Ethernet support, as a standard switch will not supply power.

stories.story:
The US Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday in Salazar v. Paramount Global, a case that could widen privacy liability for websites that use tracking tools on video pages. According to reports cited in the article, the justices appeared inclined to side with the plaintiff, while Paramount's case did not seem to persuade them.

The plaintiff alleges that a Meta tracking tool known as the Pixel on a Paramount website sent details of the videos he watched to Facebook without his consent. He wants to bring a class action seeking up to $2,500 per person under the Video Privacy Protection Act, a 1988 law passed after a journalist published the video rental history of Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork.

Paramount's lawyer, Paul Clement, argued that the plaintiff's reading would turn a law about video rentals into a sweeping internet privacy regime, and warned that sites might have to put videos behind consent walls. Justice Kagan suggested websites had two simple options, obtaining consent or stopping the sale of private data. Justice Sotomayor said gating videos would leave the choice to users. Justice Kavanaugh questioned whether it was right to repurpose a video law for web advertising tracking, and said consent would be over-broad.

If the plaintiff wins, the article says more lawsuits could follow against sites using tracking tools on video pages. The article also notes that Paramount, which recently won approval for its Warner Bros deal, is not the only media company facing viewer lawsuits, with Twitch and Amazon facing a separate class action over AI training on livestreams. A decision is expected by next summer.

stories.headline: 300-plus local data center bans have only delayed just three US projects
stories.claim: A SemiAnalysis report says over 300 local data centre moratoriums have delayed only a small share of planned US capacity.
stories.summary: SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data centre moratoriums have had little effect on US buildout, with only about 2.3 GW of 21 GW in moratorium areas likely to be delayed. Its 2027 forecast of 38 GW has barely moved in 12 months. The firm says moratoriums would need to be far more widespread and restrictive to slow the buildout. It also flags a Texas state-level pause on permits as a factor it has not fully counted.
key_points: Only about 2.3 GW of 21 GW in moratorium areas is likely to be delayed, according to SemiAnalysis.
The 2027 US data centre IT capacity forecast stands at 38 GW, more than double 2026.
Over 400 local moratorium measures are tracked across 17 states as of September.
Moratoriums often miss the site, permit or timeline, and do not revoke existing approvals.
A Texas Commission on Environmental Quality pause on data centre permits is not included in the 2.3 GW figure.

stories.story:
A report from SemiAnalysis, shared on X and summarised by Tom's Hardware, argues that more than 300 local data centre construction moratoriums have done little to slow the US buildout. Of about 21 GW of data centre capacity located in moratorium areas, the firm estimates only around 2.3 GW is likely to be delayed. Its forecast of 38 GW of US data centre IT capacity for 2027, more than double 2026, has barely moved over the past year.

The firm defines a moratorium as a temporary legal pause, usually a freeze on accepting new applications. It tracks more than 400 local measures across 17 states, including some permanent zoning bans. New York, Texas, Pennsylvania and Oregon all acted within under two months this summer. The analysis found that moratoriums often do not reach the parcel, overlap the timeline or cover a project's use, and they do not revoke existing approvals. Michigan, for example, has 45 enacted moratoriums but effectively no pipeline exposure.

The report also highlights a Texas state pause. Governor Greg Abbott told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits for data centre projects, and law firm Bracewell expects it to last until the grid operator ERCOT completes its review in mid-December. The 2.3 GW figure excludes this pause, so the analysis may understate the effect. The article says the firm would be more worried by a strict state-level moratorium that also blocked off-grid projects.

SemiAnalysis concludes that moratoriums could delay the buildout but are not yet at scale. An Economist reporter quoted in the piece described them as much more bark than bite for now, with the bigger risk being a deterrent to newer projects. Public sentiment is also a factor, with an August poll by the firm showing more negative than positive views of data centres. The next checkpoint is a TCEQ compliance report to the governor's office.
stories.market_take: The analysis suggests the US data centre buildout is largely intact, though the Texas permit pause is a watch point for energy and infrastructure names.

stories.story:

The threshold is a risk of at least $1 billion in damages, or the killing or injuring of more than 50 people. An independent third party registered with the Department of Commerce would evaluate the lab and its models periodically, and the lab could pay for those evaluations as long as this did not compromise the evaluator's independence.

The proposal names three categories of risk: the creation or release of a bioweapon, AI-enabled or AI-assisted cyberattacks, and an AI lab losing control of a model or agents. If an evaluator sees a possible such event, it must report to the Commerce Department within 72 hours. The department would then present the evidence to a federal judge in the District Court for the District of Columbia, who would decide whether the release should be halted. The bill would also bar other departments, agencies or officers from ordering an AI lab to stop releasing a model.

An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill reflects the company's Advanced AI Framework, which it has pushed with federal and state lawmakers since June, and described the policies as sensible. The article places the proposal in a climate of growing concern about AI safety, citing reported incidents involving OpenAI models, comments from Anthropic's chief executive about botnet risks, and a congressional proposal to require kill switches on the most powerful models.

The piece also mentions a separate proposal from Senator Bernie Sanders that would impose a 20-year prison term for developing AI superintelligence. The Anthropic bill would be one more measure for Congress to consider, and it is not yet law. The article does not give a timetable for a vote.
stories.market_take: Any federal AI safety rules could affect AI developers, though the proposal is at an early stage.

stories.claim: Google says 96.6% of the top Android apps run on Intel Googlebooks, while Intel and Google dispute the cause of compatibility gaps.
stories.summary: Google and Intel are publicly disagreeing over app performance on Intel-based Googlebooks, a line of Android laptops. Google says a small number of complex apps, mainly games using Arm-only native code, need developer tuning, and that 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used apps run without issues on Intel Googlebooks. Intel responded by pointing to its Intel Bridge Technology translation layer and said it expects strong compatibility and fast performance. The article explains that Arm-based Snapdragon Googlebooks avoid translation, while Intel models must translate Arm instructions in real time, which can reduce frame rates in demanding native apps. The article advises buyers to check processor type before purchase.

Just over 300 popular apps are unavailable, mostly because they do not suit large screens, Google says.

stories.story:
Google and Intel have publicly traded views on whether Android apps run well on Googlebooks, the Android-based laptops launched in October 2026. Google told Android Authority that most Android apps run smoothly on both Intel and Qualcomm models, but that a small number of complex apps or games need developer tuning on Intel hardware. It said it is working with developers, Intel and Qualcomm to improve compatibility. In a later statement it put a figure on the issue, saying 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used apps run without problems on Intel Googlebooks.

Intel responded to Gizmodo by stressing its Intel Bridge Technology. It said the translation layer uses the same underlying technology as ChromeOS but without a virtualised runtime, and that it expects users to see strong app compatibility and fast performance. The chipmaker credited its work on the Android framework and its Linux and open-source expertise. The article notes that about 300 popular apps are unavailable on Intel models, though Google says most of these are missing because they do not work on large screens rather than because of the chip.

The disagreement comes down to chip architecture. Android was built around Arm processors, and many apps, particularly games, contain native code compiled only for Arm. Dell and HP Googlebooks use Qualcomm's Arm-based Snapdragon X Elite, which runs this code directly. Acer, ASUS and Lenovo models use Intel's x86-based Panther Lake chips, which must translate Arm instructions in real time. On older Intel Chromebooks this approach felt sluggish, and the new Googlebook system removes the virtual machine but keeps the translation step. Apps written in Java or Kotlin generally run without trouble, so the issue mainly affects performance-heavy native code.

For buyers, the practical advice is to check the processor before purchase. Everyday tasks and streaming should be fine on Intel models, while demanding games such as Genshin Impact and emulators may struggle. Both companies are expected to release updates to narrow the gaps, though the timing is not stated.
stories.market_take: The dispute could slightly weigh on Intel's Googlebook appeal against Qualcomm-based models.

stories.headline: World Bank backs ‘small AI’ on phones for poorer nations, Guardian reports
stories.claim: The World Bank is encouraging developing countries to adopt compact 'small AI' models that run on basic phones.
stories.summary: The World Bank's chief knowledge officer, Paschal Donohoe, has urged developing countries to build 'small AI', which are compact, task-specific models that run on phones with weak signals. He said such tools could speed up growth in emerging economies if they fit local needs and languages. He gave the example of Indian farmers needing soil analysis in their own language. The IMF's Kristalina Georgieva said governments must first provide power, digital infrastructure and protection from bad actors. The article also notes large infrastructure gaps and warns that AI could change or remove 40% of jobs worldwide over time.

He argues AI could bring growth within decades that might otherwise take centuries.
Indian farmers in the World Bank's AgriConnect scheme are cited as a use case for soil analysis.

stories.story:
The World Bank wants developing countries to focus on what it calls 'small AI': compact models trained on narrow data for a single task, which can run on a mobile phone even when the signal is weak. Paschal Donohoe, the bank's chief knowledge officer and a former Irish finance minister, said the technology could speed up growth in emerging economies, provided it suits local needs. He suggested that development that might once have taken centuries could happen within decades.

Donohoe gave the example of farmers in India within the bank's AgriConnect scheme, who need soil analysis in their own language. He argued there will never be enough agricultural experts to serve every small farm, and said such products could come from the World Bank, governments and private firms working together. The remarks followed discussions on AI at the World Bank and IMF meetings in Bangkok earlier this month.

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said governments must first put in place power, digital infrastructure and protection from bad actors. She argued that if these basics are in place, AI adoption could be as democratic as the mobile phone. The gaps are large, however. A World Bank report from August found almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa had no electricity. Georgieva also warned that around 40% of jobs worldwide could be changed or eliminated by AI over time, with young people starting out facing the greatest risk as entry-level roles shrink.

Donohoe said the bank had raised $120bn in private capital over the past year at a time when countries including the US and UK have reduced aid budgets. The article is based on a Guardian report and the remarks are policy aspirations rather than announced programmes with set funding.
