A report says Nvidia is developing a custom form of high-bandwidth memory, called NVHBM, and has asked the major memory makers to change how they build it. Under the proposal, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix would make the base die of the memory stack on TSMC's 3nm process, rather than each using their own process. The core die would use the sixth-generation 1c DRAM process. The idea is that one common base die would make performance more consistent and mean Nvidia does not need to separately verify each supplier's samples, saving time.

The story rests on a single unnamed report and has not been confirmed by Nvidia, Samsung, Micron, SK hynix or TSMC. stories.story:
WIRED reports that the data centre industry is trying to win over younger people as public opposition to large data centres grows. The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International promotes a children's story called 'What is a Data Center?', in which a honey badger is shown around a facility. It also runs an 'International Data Center Day', offering school materials such as crosswords, colouring pages and science projects, plus books for young readers.

The activity goes beyond printed material. In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management sponsored flag-making kits for 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, which is known as Data Center Alley. The children also received a card with statistics about the industry's local economic benefits. WIRED also counted at least eleven companies and industry groups that have hosted student field trips to local data centres since 2025. Sabey, Amazon and others are among those named, and some districts describe the visits as long-standing partnerships offering talks, mock interviews and internships.

WIRED notes that industries facing reputational problems, including tobacco, fast food, and oil and gas, have long used schools for messaging. Alex Molnar, a researcher at the University of Colorado Boulder, describes the practice as corporate messaging aimed at telling a company's story rather than selling a product. He questioned what children gain from such visits. Several of the companies and schools did not respond to WIRED's requests for comment, and the article also points out that one school blog image was labelled as AI-generated.

The story matters for the wider debate over data centres, which are central to US midterm politics because of their energy and water use and their local impact. The piece suggests the sector is shifting from lobbying and tax incentives toward community and education efforts. It does not show that these programmes change local planning decisions.

stories.headline: MIT engineers build soft 3D shape-sensing skin for gaming and VR
stories.claim: MIT engineers built a soft, fibre-based sheet that senses its own 3D shape, aimed at gaming, VR and physical therapy.
stories.summary: MIT researchers have developed a soft wearable sheet that uses optical waveguides to sense its own three-dimensional shape. The sheet keeps shape-tracking error below half a centimetre in lab tests and still works when some fibres are damaged. The fibres are currently around 1 mm thick, which makes them thicker than ideal for garments. The team published the work in Advanced Intelligent Systems and sees uses in physical therapy, VR, and robot teleoperation. The work is at research stage with no commercial products announced.
key_points: The sheet uses 14 flexible optical waveguides to reconstruct 3D shape about three times a second.
Lab tests show errors below half a centimetre, with real-sheet tests giving 0.28 to 0.45 cm.
The design still functions with up to three fibres disabled, with errors rising beyond that.
Fibres are about 1 mm thick, and the team plans thinner versions for garments.
Potential uses include physical therapy tracking, VR motion control, and robot teleoperation.
stories.story:
Researchers at MIT have built a soft, wearable sheet that can sense its own three-dimensional shape. The device uses optical fibres embedded in silicone, with each fibre carrying light from an LED at one end to a sensor at the other. When the sheet bends, the amount of light that gets through changes, and an algorithm turns these readings into a full 3D shape. The team describes the work in a paper titled around fully soft, multifunctional shape sensing, published in Advanced Intelligent Systems.

In the prototype, 14 waveguides, each 160 mm long, sit in two layers within a 16 by 16 by 0.5 cm sheet. The fibres use a flexible rubber core rather than glass, and one side of each fibre is roughened so that bending in different directions causes different light losses. This allows the sheet to sense direction. The reconstruction runs in MATLAB about three times a second. In lab tests, the error stayed below half a centimetre, and in one test with three moulds of known shape the root-mean-square error ranged from 0.28 to 0.45 cm. In simulation, the error stayed under 0.3 cm with up to three fibres disabled, rising to about 1 cm or more from five disabled.

The researchers say the fully soft design may be safer around people than rigid sensors, which the lead student put at roughly 1 to 2 cm in error. Co-author Kaitlyn Becker said the team hopes to build tools that help physical therapists track patient progress. The technology could also be used for VR motion, teleoperating robots or soft robots. The current fibres are about 1 mm thick, which limits garment use, so the team plans to target a thinner sheet and says fibres could eventually get down to tens of micrometres.

The work is still at the research stage. The wearable demonstrations were carried out by one author on their own body, and the sheet does not yet measure force calibrated in units. Future work includes a faster solver than MATLAB, more waveguide layers, and a separate sheet that could sense force and shape at once. No commercial product or timeline has been announced.

stories.headline: Why are internet upload speeds so much slower than download speeds?
stories.claim: Explainer on why home internet upload speeds are much slower than download speeds, citing usage patterns and cable limits.
stories.summary: Engadget explains why home internet upload speeds usually lag far behind download speeds. Most people download far more than they upload, and cable networks built for TV allocate most capacity to downloads. Fibre connections, by contrast, typically offer equal speeds in both directions. The article also notes that content delivery networks help downloads but have no real equivalent for uploads. It is an explainer rather than a news event, so it has no direct market angle.
key_points: Typical cable plans in the example offer around 117 Mbps upload regardless of download tier up to 1 Gbps.
Most internet activity, such as streaming and app updates, is download-heavy.
Cable uses coaxial copper designed for one-way TV, and DOCSIS upgrades are costly for ISPs.
Fibre can offer equal upload and download speeds because of its much greater capacity.
Content delivery networks speed up downloads, but uploads lack an equivalent shortcut.
stories.story:
Engadget has explained why home internet upload speeds are typically much slower than download speeds. The article uses an example of a US cable provider where three download tiers, 300 Mbps, 500 Mbps and 1 Gbps, all share a typical upload speed of 117 Mbps. Only a 2 Gbps plan lifts upload to around 293 Mbps. The explanation combines how people use the internet with the physical limits of the networks that carry it.

The main practical reason is behaviour. Most people download far more than they upload, whether streaming video, installing apps and updates, or loading web pages. The article argues that most households do not need fast uploads unless they regularly send large files, stream live or run several video calls at once, so providers allocate most of their capacity to downloads.

The physical medium also matters. Standard cable internet uses coaxial copper lines originally designed for one-way television. The DOCSIS standard lets these lines carry internet traffic in both directions, and newer versions improve speeds, but upgrading equipment is expensive for providers. Cable neighbourhoods also share capacity, so speeds can slow at busy times. Fibre, which uses light, has far greater capacity and so usually offers symmetrical speeds.

Finally, content delivery networks let companies such as Netflix and Google store copies of popular content near users, which eases the load on networks for downloads. Uploads usually travel to a single destination and are often unique files, so there is no equivalent shortcut, which places more work on ISP infrastructure. The piece is an explainer and does not report a new development or any company decision.

stories.headline: Two German courts now hold Google liable for what its AI overviews say
stories.claim: A second German court, in Aachen, held Google liable for false statements in its AI Mode search answers, following a Munich precedent.
stories.summary: A second German court, the Aachen Regional Court, has issued an emergency injunction against Google over false statements generated by its AI Mode search feature. The court relied on the reasoning of an earlier Munich ruling that treated Google's AI answers as the company's own content. The decision is not final and Google can challenge it. The case is part of a wider legal debate over whether AI search companies are responsible for what their systems generate.
key_points: The Aachen court issued a decision dated September 24, 2026 barring Google from spreading three disputed text variants.
A physician said AI Mode wrongly linked him to misconduct and legal proceedings involving a different former professor.
Google reportedly said in mid-September it would take no action after the doctor's complaint and formal legal demand.
The court cited the Munich ruling, which treated AI Overviews as Google's own statements.
Violations could cost up to 250,000 euros each, and the injunction can still be challenged.
stories.story:
A German court in Aachen has ordered Google to stop spreading certain false statements generated by its AI Mode search feature. The Regional Court acted on an emergency basis, in a decision dated September 24, 2026, without first hearing from Google. The case involves a physician who was chief physician and professor of neuroradiology until late June 2026. He says that, from late August, the AI was attributing to him a sexual assault allegation and invented legal proceedings that in fact concerned a different former university professor.

The doctor says he asked Google by email to remove the content and sent a formal legal demand in mid-September. According to the court, Google said it would take no action and the false texts remained live. The court banned the spread of three disputed text variants. Breaching the order could cost Google up to 250,000 euros per violation. The decision is not final, and Google can challenge it.

The ruling follows an earlier Munich Regional Court decision in May, which found Google directly liable for false claims in AI Overviews, classing them as the company's own statements rather than neutral search results. Google had announced an appeal in that case, but the matter was later settled, so no higher court has ruled on the reasoning. The Aachen judges explicitly relied on the Munich logic, describing Google's AI outputs as independent, new statements drawn from multiple third-party sites.

The ruling could have wider consequences for AI search businesses in Germany and elsewhere, since it challenges the idea that a search engine is only a neutral intermediary. Commentators note that if such liability holds, publishers whose content feeds AI answers might also make claims. Google has not, in the material reviewed, commented publicly on the Aachen decision, and the broader legal strategy for its AI search features remains open to question.
stories.market_take: Potential legal risk for Alphabet's AI search business in Germany, though the financial impact is currently unclear.

stocks.reason: Legal exposure for AI Mode and AI Overviews answers could raise costs and compliance risk in Germany.

stories.headline: Biotech now sells pet cloning and cryonics, MIT Technology Review finds
stories.claim: MIT Technology Review reports that pet biotech now includes longevity drugs, cloning at $50,000, and cryonics for dogs and cats.
stories.summary: MIT Technology Review has outlined a growing set of biotech options for pet owners, including longevity drugs, cloning and cryopreservation. Loyal is testing a daily pill for senior dogs in about 1,300 dogs, and US regulators have accepted its safety data as a step towards approval. Viagen Pets reportedly charges $50,000 to clone a cat or dog. Some firms freeze dead pets in the hope of future revival, though experts say this is highly unlikely. The article is a feature rather than a corporate announcement.
key_points: Loyal is testing LOY-002, a daily pill for senior dogs, in about 1,300 pet dogs in the US.
US regulators accepted Loyal's safety data in January, but this is not full approval.
Loyal expects to apply for conditional approval in 2027.
Viagen Pets reportedly charges $50,000 to clone a cat or dog.
Alcor in Arizona stores hundreds of pets and people, and experts consider revival highly unlikely.
stories.story:
A feature from MIT Technology Review, summarised by The Next Web, looks at the growing range of biotechnology options available to pet owners. These include longevity drugs for animals, cloning services and cryonic preservation. The piece questions whether some of these options are wise, while also setting out the grief-related reasons owners might pursue them.

The longevity option is led by the US startup Loyal, which is developing three drugs for dogs. Its lead candidate, LOY-002, is a daily pill for senior dogs and is being tested in about 1,300 pet dogs across the United States. In January, regulators accepted the company's safety data for the drug. This is a step towards approval rather than approval itself, and Loyal expects to apply for conditional approval in 2027. Other companies are testing treatments for age-related conditions such as obesity and arthritis in dogs, and one is developing longevity medicines for cats.

Cloning is also available. The process takes DNA from a pet and places it in an egg from another animal of the same species, with a surrogate carrying the embryo. Texas-based Viagen Pets reportedly charges $50,000 to clone a cat or dog. The resulting animal is a genetic twin rather than a copy with the same personality. A Colorado State University professor who studies human-animal bonds suggested that owners facing grief should not be judged for seeking such comfort.

Cryonics is the most speculative option. Alcor in Arizona stores hundreds of pets and people, and has recently frozen its first pet sugar glider. Experts say revival is highly unlikely. The magazine's Jessica Hamzelou said she was concerned that cloning and cryonics could give children the impression that death is not final. The article also notes that startups such as HexemBio are raising money for human rejuvenation therapies, reflecting a wider push against ageing in biotech.

stories.summary: The Verge reports that cities and states across the political spectrum are introducing their own rules to restrict or shape robotaxi operations because Congress has not passed federal autonomous vehicle legislation. Minneapolis is considering a human-monitor requirement, San Diego has sought to block Waymo from its airport, and California lawmakers are weighing several bills. stories.story:
Cities and states across the political spectrum are introducing their own rules to govern robotaxis, as federal regulators work on safety standards and Congress has yet to pass legislation setting national rules for autonomous vehicles. The article describes a growing patchwork of local laws that operators must navigate, an outcome the industry had hoped to avoid.

Several examples are cited. Minneapolis is considering an ordinance requiring human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council has passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport. Austin firefighters have raised concerns about the Tesla Cybercab's lack of steering wheel or pedals and want rapid-response towing protocols. In California, lawmakers are weighing bills that would let cities limit fleet sizes, restrict operating hours and impose permit bans, while some local areas have used zoning and noise rules to restrict charging hubs.

The pushback is cutting across party lines. Some Democrat-led cities still do not allow driverless cars, and several Republican-led states, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota and Iowa, are reported to be considering tighter rules. Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing but hold broad power over street operations, which is why they are acting.

In response, developers are looking abroad. Waymo plans to expand in London, Tokyo and Munich, and Uber is preparing vehicles for Manchester, Madrid and Dubai. Operators are also favouring states that pre-empt city bans. The article suggests that any federal law is unlikely to strip cities of their core powers, so companies should expect the patchwork to continue.

stories.story:
Intel has laid out its vision for silicon photonics at the OCP 2026 conference, presenting the technology as the next major system architecture for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence. Nic Dubé, the company's corporate vice president for data centre systems and solutions, described silicon photonics as the "golden hammer" of next-generation systems. He said talks about making it an industry standard have been under way for some time, and that Intel is working to make it a reality within the next couple of years.

The company argues that conventional electrical links over copper are running into limits on reach, bandwidth per shoreline and energy per bit, and that silicon photonics addresses all three. Intel's central claim is that it is the only high-volume chip fab able to deliver 300mm indium phosphide silicon photonics at scale for the wider industry. It says these wafers will carry the advanced silicon needed for future co-packaged and near-packaged optical functions in AI and HPC.

Intel also highlighted integrated lasers, which would remove the need for servicing a separate light source, and said it plans to support external light-source standards that could bring multi-wavelength light sources made in a US fab. Beyond raw bandwidth, it described interconnect topologies that orchestrate resources across CPUs, GPUs and memory pools at runtime. The company estimates that photonics could bring energy per bit below 5 picojoules, which it describes as a long-awaited goal.

The presentation is a pitch rather than a product launch, and Intel gave no commercial timeline beyond the next couple of years. The company said it hopes to work with partners to bring the technology to market, so the practical outcome will depend on ecosystem adoption.
stories.market_take: Positive for Intel's foundry ambitions, but the claims are early-stage and the benefit to its share price is uncertain.

stories.headline: Anthropic has nearly stopped hiring junior staff because AI agents now work six times as many hours
stories.claim: Anthropic's internal study says junior hiring in its technical teams has fallen as its AI agents log far more hours than staff.
stories.summary: Anthropic has published an internal study showing its share of junior technical roles fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025, with the share among new hires dropping from 27% to 9%. The company links the trend to its AI agents, which by August 2026 were logging six times as many work hours as human employees. The study reports productivity gains across departments, but its author acknowledges Anthropic is a special case. Researchers warn that cutting entry-level roles could weaken the future pool of experienced talent.
key_points: Junior share of technical roles at Anthropic fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025.
Junior share of new technical hires fell from 27% to 9%, with a sharp drop from December 2025.
By August 2026, Anthropic's AI agents were logging six times as many work hours as human employees.
Reported productivity gains include 5.1 times as many code commits for engineers and 1.7 times as many closed sales deals.
The study concedes Anthropic is an unusually AI-heavy firm, so results may not generalise to the wider economy.
A researcher warns the long-term cost of losing entry-level training may only appear between 2030 and 2045.
stories.story:
Anthropic has released an internal study showing that it is hiring fewer junior staff in its technical departments as its AI agents take on a growing share of work. According to the study, junior positions in technical teams fell from 21% to 14% of the total since early 2025. Among new hires alone, the junior share dropped more steeply, from 27% to 9%, with open junior roles falling especially sharply from December 2025 onwards.

The company attributes this to the growing capability of its AI agents. By August 2026, those agents were logging six times as many work hours as Anthropic's human staff. Tasks such as writing code and finding bugs are increasingly passed to its Claude models, and junior hiring fell most in the roles where Claude handled the most complex work. The study also reports productivity gains across every department, including 5.1 times as many code commits from engineers and 1.7 times as many closed sales deals.

The study itself acknowledges limits. Anthropic is an extremely AI-heavy software company, so its results may not map onto the broader economy, and rapid growth and voluntary adoption of AI tools could also be distorting the figures. The article notes that the wider economy has not yet shown measurable productivity gains from AI.

The piece also cites researcher Nolan Lovett, who describes a "tragedy of the cognitive commons": firms gain efficiency by replacing entry-level roles, while the cost of having too few experienced workers falls on everyone later. Lovett argues the full impact may not show until 2030 to 2045, and that software engineering, financial analysis and legal research are the most exposed fields. The article adds that this forecast assumes humans still do such work, which Anthropic has itself suggested may not be the case in the long run.
stories.market_take: The study hints at labour-cost savings from AI for AI-heavy software firms, but it is company-specific and offers little direct market signal.

stories.story:
Android Police has published an opinion piece arguing that Google's new Fitbit Edge does not find a clear place in the company's wearables range. Google has recently released the screenless Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, and the Edge is pitched as a fitness wearable that sits between the two. The author argues that it does not stand out clearly from either.

The Fitbit Air is described as a screenless tracker that counts steps, monitors heart rate and sleep, and relies on automatic sensors, with exercise logged through the Google Health app. The Edge adds a small 1.34-inch AMOLED display with an always-on option, which the author sees as its main difference. The Pixel Watch 5, by contrast, is a full smartwatch with apps, Gemini, messaging and, with LTE, the ability to act as a phone replacement.

The author's central complaint is that the Edge lacks the features that define the Pixel Watch 5 while also offering far less of the appeal of the Air. The piece compares this to the basic Galaxy S phone, which struggles to stand out next to the Plus and Ultra models. The author says the Edge is effectively a Fitbit Charge 7 released in a market where the Air is a newer, bolder product.

The article does not suggest the device is poor. It notes that the Edge is likely to be a good tracker, and manufacturer copy presents it as a solid option at a good price. The author's view is that its success is doubtful, and that it may have lost its place before launch. The piece is opinion rather than a report on sales or market reception.

stories.headline: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale’s UK data centre weeks before its IPO
stories.claim: Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, ahead of Nscale's IPO.
stories.summary: The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The move comes as the AI cloud startup prepares an IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong. Microsoft has not commented, and the site has faced grid connection delays. The story also covers wider investor caution around neocloud firms.
key_points: The Telegraph reports Microsoft has walked away from anchoring Nscale's Loughton data centre, with no reason given.
Authorities have reportedly told Nscale that power may not arrive until the 2030s.
Nscale is seeking up to $3bn in an IPO as soon as this month.

Nscale says the Microsoft relationship is strong and the grid issue does not affect its other contracts.
CoreWeave shares fell 25% last week, reflecting wariness toward neocloud firms.
stories.story:
The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor the first British data centre of Nscale, the AI cloud startup, in Loughton, Essex. The move comes as Nscale prepares to go public, and Bloomberg, citing the Telegraph, says the site has faced a series of delays. The Telegraph did not give a reason for Microsoft's decision. Microsoft did not comment to the Telegraph and did not immediately respond to Bloomberg.

The Loughton site has been affected by grid problems. Authorities have reportedly told Nscale not to expect a power supply until the 2030s. The Next Web had reported in July that the grid could not connect the site in time for its planned opening. Nscale says it remains committed to the site, is looking at other power sources and UK locations, and that its relationship with Microsoft is strong and long-term. It says the grid issue does not affect its other contracts.

The IPO is significant. Nscale is seeking to raise as much as $3bn, possibly as soon as this month. Its filing shows Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of its contracts. Anthropic agreed in August to spend $45bn on Nscale compute over six years, and Microsoft has signed a letter of intent for a campus in West Virginia. Bloomberg also reports that Nscale's flagship Norway site is six months behind schedule, with only 6.4 megawatts of a planned 30-megawatt facility running.

The wider context is investor caution about neocloud companies, which are racing to build AI computing capacity and often borrow heavily. CoreWeave shares fell 25% last week, their worst week since November, and Australia's Firmus scrapped its IPO after failing to win enough support. Whether Microsoft's withdrawal is confirmed, and how Nscale's listing is priced, will be closely watched.

Nscale responded without denying the withdrawal
Microsoft did not comment
stories.market_take: Weakens confidence in Nscale's IPO and in neocloud peers, which may weigh on CoreWeave and similar stocks.

stories.headline: Startup makes tiny 'benchtop' fusion devices for more efficient reactors
stories.claim: Startup Cambridge Heavy Industries has unveiled a benchtop laser fusion device aimed at producing tritium rather than electricity.
stories.summary: Cambridge Heavy Industries, a startup operating in stealth from a lab linked to MIT, has shared details of a compact laser fusion device. The system uses two lasers in a 2D setup and is designed to run 50 to 80 experiments per day. Its immediate focus is making tritium, a fuel for fusion, rather than generating electricity. The article estimates a tritium shortfall of up to 28 kg by 2054 across the industry.
key_points: Cambridge Heavy Industries describes its fusion device as tiny and benchtop-sized.
It uses two lasers: the first compresses fuel with inward shock waves, the second triggers ignition.
The device can run 50 to 80 laser shots per day, compared with a handful at the NIF.
The immediate goal is producing tritium, not electricity.
A study cited by TechCrunch suggests a tritium shortfall of up to 28 kg by 2054, worth about $840m at today's prices.
Practical fusion electricity is still some years away.
stories.story:
Cambridge Heavy Industries, a startup that has been operating in stealth from a laboratory attached to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has begun to describe its fusion technology. Co-founder and chief executive Yun Kai describes the device as tiny and benchtop-sized, which the company says allows experiments to be run and refined quickly. The aim is to eventually build something about the size of two basketball courts, far smaller than conventional power plants.

The company's approach uses two lasers. The first delivers light in concentric rings that drive shock waves inwards to compress a block of fuel. The second laser strikes the compressed wave at the right moment to reach the pressure needed for ignition. The design is two-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, so it needs fewer angles of attack than the 192-laser setup at the National Ignition Facility in the United States. The company says its device can carry out 50 to 80 laser shots a day, while the NIF manages only a handful.

The device is not yet designed to generate electricity. Its immediate focus is tritium, one of the two fuels expected to be used in fusion. Tritium is scarce and comes mainly from ageing nuclear fission plants being phased out. Reactors that could breed their own tritium are not expected before the 2030s at the earliest, which the company sees as a window of opportunity.

Citing a recent study, TechCrunch reports that the global tritium shortfall could reach 28 kilograms by 2054, worth roughly $840 million at today's prices. The article stresses that fusion has been produced in laboratories for decades but has not yet been used to generate electricity practically, and that this remains years away. The company's approach is still at an early stage, and the article does not report independent verification of its performance.
stories.market_take: Early-stage private fusion firm with no listed stake; little direct market effect.

stories.headline: Cinebench world record that stood for 12 years gets toppled
stories.claim: An overclocker set a new HWBot Cinebench R11.5 record for the Core i5 4670K using liquid nitrogen cooling.
stories.summary: Overclocker Luumi has taken the HWBot Cinebench R11.5 record for the Intel Core i5 4670K, a Haswell-era quad-core chip, after 12 years. The multicore score of 10.8 cb was achieved with liquid nitrogen cooling, with the CPU reaching about 6.3 GHz. The result applies only to the i5 4670K category rather than all quad-core processors. The article also notes that a modern laptop scored roughly four times higher in the same test.
key_points: Overclocker Luumi set a new HWBot Cinebench R11.5 record in the Core i5 4670K category.
The previous record had stood for about 12 years and the new multicore score is 10.8 cb.
The system used an ASRock Z97 OC Formula motherboard, 4GB of XPG DDR3 memory and liquid nitrogen cooling.
The CPU reportedly ran at about 6,301 MHz according to validation files.
The test ran on Windows 7 64-bit, and the older Cinebench still runs on Windows 11.
stories.story:
An overclocker known as Luumi has set a new world record on HWBot for Cinebench R11.5 using an Intel Core i5 4670K, a Haswell-era processor first released about a decade ago. The record score is a multicore result of 10.8 cb, which knocks off a mark that had stood for roughly 12 years. The run relied on liquid nitrogen cooling, and validation files show the chip running at about 6,301 MHz. The system was built around an ASRock Z97 OC Formula motherboard with 4GB of XPG DDR3 memory and a Corsair power supply.

The record is specific to the Core i5 4670K category, not to all quad-core processors. The i5 4670K is an unlocked four-core, four-thread chip with a stock boost of 3.8 GHz and a 84W rating, built on Intel's 22nm process. Higher-end chips of the era with eight threads were sold as i7 models. The article's author noted that the result is a good example of older hardware still being competitive in overclocking circles.

The article also includes a comparison by the author, who ran the same older benchmark on a modern 12-core, 24-thread laptop and recorded a score about four times higher. The author noted that the older Cinebench still works without trouble on Windows 11. Some older 3DMark tests, however, have compatibility issues with modern systems, which can make their results invalid for HWBot rankings.

The story is a niche hardware achievement with no real market significance. It highlights how enthusiast benchmarking continues to celebrate older components rather than the latest flagship parts.

stories.story:

The company describes it as a fully autonomous, tracked machine that carries solar module pallets from storage areas to installation rows, reducing the need for human operators or flagmen on site.

The machine combines GPS positioning, laser-based mapping, 3D computer vision and 360-degree LiDAR to find pallets and plan its route. It is powered by a 48-volt lithium battery with a nominal capacity of 19.2 kWh, which the company says supports about eight hours of continuous operation under standard conditions. The tracked design and IP67 rating are intended to allow use on sand, gravel, mud and icy ground. It is rated to carry up to 3,000 kg per load.

LEAPTING claims the robot can mount modules on trackers every 40 seconds, which it says is three to five times faster than manual labour, with placement accuracy under 1 mm. These figures come from the company and have not been independently verified in the article. The launch fits a wider trend of automating solar construction as developers seek to cut labour costs and safety risks on large projects.

stories.headline: Your smart TV has one big problem: It's tracking what you watch
stories.claim: Smart TVs use automatic content recognition to track viewing habits, and the article explains how users can limit it.
stories.summary: An Engadget guide explains that smart TVs use Automatic Content Recognition to capture screenshots and audio to identify what viewers watch. The data can be uploaded to manufacturers and sold to data brokers, and the ACR market is forecast to reach $23.37 billion by 2034. Manufacturers say the practice keeps TV prices low and is disclosed during setup. The article offers steps for switching ACR off, while warning that settings may be re-enabled by updates.
key_points: Smart TVs use Automatic Content Recognition to capture screenshots several times a second to identify viewing.
Data can include IP addresses, Wi-Fi details, app usage and voice snippets.
Vizio's Platform+ business made $598 million in 2023, according to the article.
Analysts forecast the ACR market will reach $23.37 billion by 2034.
Settings may be re-enabled after software updates, and some TVs keep collecting data while offline.
stories.story:
Engadget has published a guide on how smart TVs track what people watch and how viewers can limit it. Most smart TVs use Automatic Content Recognition, which takes frequent screenshots and identifies what appears on built-in apps, streaming services and connected devices such as game consoles. The technology can also gather technical information like IP addresses, Wi-Fi details and app usage. Voice-enabled remotes may send short audio clips for processing.

The collected data is turned into a digital fingerprint and sent to the manufacturer. It may then be sold to data brokers who combine it with other information. The article cites Vizio's Platform+ business, which includes free ad-supported TV, as having made $598 million in 2023. Analysts quoted in the piece expect the ACR market to reach $23.37 billion by 2034. Manufacturers argue that ACR revenue helps keep TV prices down and say the feature is disclosed during setup.

Critics say the switch-off options are hard to find and that the practice is not made clear to buyers. In some cases state privacy laws require more openness, and there has been litigation in Texas against large TV makers. The guide notes that manufacturers use different names and controls for ACR, and that turning it off may affect other TV features.

The article advises readers to check their settings again after software updates, since ACR may be re-enabled. It also says some TVs keep capturing data while offline and upload it when reconnected. Beyond the main toggles, it offers further steps to limit data collection.

stocks.reason: Privacy scrutiny of smart TV data practices could affect TV makers, though the effect is likely small.

stories.headline: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?
stories.claim: Anthropic's red team reported a proof-of-concept AI worm that spread across 15 smart TVs, prompting debate on the risk.
stories.summary: Anthropic's offensive research team has published a report describing a test AI program that spread autonomously across 15 internet-connected smart TVs, sharing its functions across devices. Security experts said the weak security of smart devices makes such threats hard to fix. Other experts called the risk overstated for now, noting that the test version is slow and that basic security steps would block most attacks. A University of Toronto paper earlier this year had also shown a worm spreading between full-size computers.
key_points: Anthropic's red team built a test AI program that spread across 15 smart TVs and ran by sharing small amounts of computing power.
Experts said weak security and infrequent patching of smart devices could make AI worms hard to stop.
Anthropic researchers said a capable worm would need more capability on weak devices, which they expect may be feasible by year end.
A University of Toronto paper previously showed an AI worm infecting a full-size computer.
Other security specialists called the threat overstated and said basic measures such as strong passwords and two-factor authentication would stop most attacks.
stories.story:
Anthropic's offensive research team has reported that it built a test AI program capable of spreading itself through internet-connected smart televisions. The program divided parts of itself across 15 TVs and kept functioning by drawing a small amount of power from each. The researchers said the same approach could work on other ordinary devices, and they argued that such self-replicating programs, known as AI worms, could become more practical by the end of the year as hardware trends improve.

Security experts quoted in the piece said the weak protection of smart TVs and other internet-connected devices would be difficult to fix, since such devices receive updates less often than phones or laptops. The Anthropic team also suggested that an AI worm could keep adapting by researching newly disclosed flaws. Historical worms such as the 1988 Morris worm, Stuxnet, NotPetya and WannaCry are cited as examples of the damage self-spreading malware can cause.

Other experts were more sceptical. A co-author of a University of Toronto study, which infected a full-size computer, said the Anthropic version moves very slowly and can be detected and blocked. Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade of SentinelOne called the work stunt hacking that is being overstated for marketing purposes. Experts said that strong passwords and two-factor authentication would stop most worms.

stories.headline: Banks could slow stablecoin growth by paying savers more, BIS paper finds
stories.claim: A BIS working paper finds that higher bank deposit rates can slow stablecoin market growth, though the effect is modest.
stories.summary: A Bank for International Settlements working paper finds that banks paying savers more can slow the growth of stablecoins such as USDT and USDC. A one basis point rise in deposit rates was linked to ten-week stablecoin growth falling from about 15% to about 12%. Under a preferred estimate the effect was larger, slowing growth to about 6%. The authors caution that the findings do not show losses of deposits or lending.
key_points: A BIS paper using data from January 2019 to June 2025 links higher bank deposit rates to slower stablecoin growth.
A one basis point rise in deposit rates cut average ten-week growth from about 15% to about 12%.
The authors' preferred estimate, adjusting for banks reacting to stablecoin growth, points to growth slowing to about 6%.
The link was stronger for Circle's USDC than for Tether's USDT, which the authors tie to USDC's closer US user base.
The paper does not establish actual deposit or lending losses, and its sample covers only one high-rate period.
stories.story:
A working paper published by the Bank for International Settlements examines whether banks can slow the growth of stablecoins by paying savers more. Researchers Rashad Ahmed and Iñaki Aldasoro analysed weekly data from January 2019 to June 2025, controlling for bitcoin prices, Treasury yields and broader financial conditions. They found that a rise of just one basis point in average bank deposit rates was followed by slower stablecoin growth.

The effect in the basic estimate was modest. A 0.01 percentage point rise cut average ten-week growth in stablecoin market capitalisation from roughly 15% to about 12%. Under the authors' preferred estimate, which accounts for banks raising rates in response to stablecoin growth, the effect was about three times larger, slowing growth to around 6%. The authors noted weaknesses in that method, but in both cases growth slowed without reversing. The relationship was stronger for Circle's USDC than for Tether's USDT, which the authors linked to USDC's closer ties to US users.

The findings add evidence to a debate that bank leaders have raised. Bank of America's chief executive, Brian Moynihan, warned in January that as much as $6 trillion in deposits could shift into stablecoins and similar products offering returns, which could reduce lending capacity and raise borrowing costs. A December Federal Reserve staff analysis also noted that money placed in stablecoins can flow back to banks as issuer deposits, changing the source of bank funding even when total deposits stay the same.

The paper is careful about its limits. It does not establish any loss of deposits or lending, and its sample covers a single high-rate episode. The authors suggest the picture could change as yield-bearing stablecoins and tokenised money market funds grow. They conclude that banks retain some influence over how quickly stablecoins are adopted through the rates they set for depositors. The working paper is a research contribution rather than a policy decision, so it signals a trade-off for banks rather than an immediate shift in the market.
stories.market_take: The research suggests higher deposit rates could curb stablecoin growth, a mild consideration for bank funding costs and crypto-linked firms.

stories.story:
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis's ruling coalition failed to win a single seat in the Senate elections, according to final results from a two-day ballot. Candidates linked to pro-Western opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member chamber. The result means the opposition keeps control of the upper house, which it already held before the vote.

The ANO movement, which Babis leads, now holds 14 Senate seats but gained no new ones in this round. Babis said his party had not expected to fail to win any seat, but said his government would still push ahead with its programme. One key plan is a controversial overhaul of how public broadcasters are funded, which the article describes as unpopular. The coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine and opposes EU climate policies.

The election was the first electoral test for Babis since he returned to power after winning parliamentary elections in October 2025. The lower house is the main legislative chamber, but the Senate has a significant role in passing constitutional amendments and approving judges for the Constitutional Court. An opposition-controlled Senate could therefore slow or block parts of the government's agenda.

The result is a political setback for Babis, though not a change in government. Attention will now turn to how the government handles the Senate's opposition and whether the broadcaster funding plan moves forward. The outcome has limited direct market impact.

stories.headline: Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest oil reserves and sends 90% of its crude exports to the U.S. — It will vote on a first step to leaving Canada
stories.claim: Alberta voters will decide on October 19 whether to begin a legal process toward a possible separation referendum from Canada.
stories.summary: Fortune, citing the Associated Press, reports that Alberta voters will decide on 19 October whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future separation referendum. Premier Danielle Smith opposes separation, and support for starting the process was around 23% in a recent poll. The separatist movement has grown from the 2022 Freedom Convoy and has met US State Department officials. Alberta sends roughly 90% of its crude exports to the United States.
key_points: Alberta votes on 19 October on whether to begin a legal process toward a separation referendum.
Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote, opposes separation, and a recent poll put support for starting the process at about 23%.
Separatist leaders say they have met US State Department officials three times, which the department says is routine.
Alberta sends about 90% of its crude oil exports to the United States and holds the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves.
Prime Minister Mark Carney is popular in Alberta and backs getting oil to new markets.
stories.story:
Voters in Alberta, Canada's main oil-producing province, will decide on 19 October whether the province should stay in Canada or start the legal process toward a future referendum on leaving. The vote does not itself decide independence. Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote, supports remaining in Canada, and has said that support for the separation process, around 23% in a recent poll, is still too high for her liking.

The article traces the roots of the movement to long-running anger over federal energy and carbon policy, and to the 2022 Freedom Convoy protests against pandemic restrictions. Former premier Jason Kenney argues that the convoy supporters shifted to separatism, and he links some activists to a wider set of political views. Separatist leader Jeff Rath says he expects well short of a majority, and hopes for more than 30% of the vote. Keith Wilson, another separatist leader, said the vote could give Alberta more leverage with Ottawa even short of independence.

The piece also highlights links to Washington. Separatist advocates say they met US State Department officials three times and presented a document on what an independent Alberta could offer the United States, and a State Department spokesperson said it meets a wide range of representatives. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a natural partner. Prime Minister Mark Carney, who backs a pipeline to the West Coast and opposes US trade pressure, is unusually popular in the province.

The article notes that Quebec returned the separatist Parti Quebecois to power on 5 October, though it is not clear from the excerpt what effect that has on Alberta. The vote is a significant political test for national unity, and its outcome could affect investor sentiment around Canadian energy and the oil sector.
stories.market_take: Investors in Canadian energy may watch the 19 October vote for signs of political risk to oil pipeline plans.

stories.headline: Reform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’
stories.claim: An undercover ITV investigation recorded a Reform UK candidate calling for asylum seekers to be put in 'concentration camps' and saying Muslims cannot be British.
stories.summary: An ITV undercover investigation recorded a would-be Reform UK MP saying asylum seekers should be placed in 'concentration camps' and that Muslims cannot be British. The footage is due to be broadcast on Sunday, and earlier excerpts showed other Reform members using racist language. Reform says it is investigating and that there is no room for racism. Councillor Alan Feeney has resigned after racist comments about Asian homeowners were uncovered. Labour has said Nigel Farage is unfit to lead.
key_points: An undercover ITV investigation recorded a Reform UK activist and would-be MP making extreme remarks about Muslims and asylum seekers.
The activist is yet to be publicly identified, and the footage is due to be broadcast on Sunday.
Reform says it has opened investigations and that there is 'no room for racism' in the party.
Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after racist comments were uncovered.
Labour's party chair said Nigel Farage was unfit to lead, while Farage said vetting cannot predict future comments.
stories.story:
An undercover ITV investigation has recorded a Reform UK activist and aspiring MP saying that Muslims cannot be British and that asylum seekers should be placed in 'concentration camps'. Further footage is due to be broadcast on Sunday, and the man has not yet been publicly named. Excerpts released earlier in the week already showed councillors and candidates from the party using racist language, including describing Black children as 'animals'.

Reform has said it has opened investigations where members have behaved inappropriately and stressed that there is no room for racism in the party. In a statement to ITV, it said it had improved its vetting process but that some individuals would still get through, and that one cannot vet future comments. Nigel Farage has made a similar point, saying vetting cannot predict what people will say in the future.

The controversy has also led to a resignation. Alan Feeney stepped down as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after ITV revealed footage of him describing Asian homeowners as 'parasites' during a local election campaign. He apologised and said his remarks were wrong and unacceptable.

Labour's party chair, Bridget Phillipson, said Farage's response showed he was unfit to lead and accused the party's leadership of sharing responsibility. The row adds to pressure on Reform, which is seeking to build its support ahead of future elections, and is likely to shape political debate in the coming days.

stories.story:
Donald Trump held a campaign rally in Highland Heights, Kentucky, on Saturday, speaking in support of Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. He said that his power in his second term was greater than in his first, claiming that he could "do stuff that is unbelievable", and pointed to a change in how the US government refers to the Gulf of Mexico. He also joked about changing the name of a lake in Canada.

The article sets his remarks against voter frustration with tariffs and the Iran war, which it links to rising prices. Trump said the war would end soon, a claim the article says he has made many times during a conflict of nearly eight months. He also repeated a promise that every adult American would receive $5,000 if Republicans win both chambers of Congress. The article estimates that such a payment would likely cost more than $1 trillion and need congressional approval, against a budget deficit of around $1.8 trillion a year.

Trump also made a conditional pledge that the Department of Defense would invest in reviving a drug manufacturing facility in Kentucky if Republicans win. He brought on stage Ed Gallrein, who defeated Representative Thomas Massie in the Republican primary. Massie had opposed the Iran war and pushed for release of Epstein files. The crowd's response to Trump's attacks on Massie was described as lukewarm.

stories.claim: Think-tank E3G says a £15bn warm homes plan would beat new North Sea oil drilling on bills, jobs and growth.
stories.summary: A study by the thinktank E3G argues that insulating homes and installing heat pumps would cut household energy bills and create far more jobs than the Rosebank oilfield. The warm homes plan is reportedly under threat of cuts. The findings have been contested by Adura, the joint venture behind Rosebank, which says the project would add significant economic value.

stories.story:
A study by the thinktank E3G suggests that insulating Britain's homes and investing in heat pumps would do more to reduce living costs, create jobs and boost the economy than drilling for new oil. The think tank puts the government's £15bn warm homes plan, which is reportedly under threat of cuts as ministers seek savings, at £1bn a year off household energy bills. It estimates the plan would add £1.6bn a year to the economy and support around 50,000 jobs across many small businesses.

By comparison, E3G says the Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland would create about 1,100 direct and indirect jobs, mostly in the North Sea and at two companies, one of them Equinor. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said a decision on the Jackdaw gasfield was imminent and that Rosebank would take a little longer. Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged to halt new oil and gas licensing, but both fields may be exceptions because they were already in the system.

Other research cited in the article, from WWF and Uplift, suggests tax revenues from Rosebank may be limited because of generous reliefs. E3G also estimates the warm homes plan would lift GDP by 0.08%, against roughly 0.025% for Rosebank on average over its life, assuming oil returns to $70 a barrel. Decommissioning costs could also be large, with taxpayers possibly asked for £12bn.

Adura, the joint venture of Equinor and Shell that owns Jackdaw and Rosebank, says approving Rosebank and other developments would support £35.3bn of UK economic value over 2026 to 2035. Its figures have been questioned because they include assumptions about spending and do not appear to apply a discount rate. Ten unions and many Labour MPs oppose Rosebank, and Energy UK has warned that watering down the warm homes plan sends mixed signals to the market. The energy department declined to comment on the study.
stories.market_take: A Rosebank approval would support Equinor and Shell, while a stronger warm homes plan would benefit insulation and heat pump suppliers.

stories.claim: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper ordered NHS England to draw up urgent plans to end corridor care for children and announced £140m for urgent care.
stories.summary: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she has asked NHS England to produce urgent plans to end children being treated in hospital corridors and to set new A&E standards for children. She also announced £140m to boost urgent care capacity ahead of a difficult winter. Waiting figures are rising, with 50,582 people waiting over 12 hours in A&E in September. The Royal College of Nursing called the funding 'just another sticking plaster'.
key_points: Cooper has asked NHS England to draw up urgent plans to eliminate corridor care for children as a priority.

stories.story:
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has told the BBC that the NHS must act urgently to stop children being treated in hospital corridors. She said she has asked NHS England to draw up plans to eliminate so-called corridor care for children as a priority, and to introduce new standards for how children are treated in A&E. Cooper said the way the data is collected will change so that children are included in the figures. The government also has a broader plan to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament.

The figures behind the announcement are stark. The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E from a decision to admit until actually being admitted rose to 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August. Almost 7.3 million people attended A&E in England between June and August, the highest figure ever recorded for a summer period, after a series of heatwaves. The waiting list for routine hospital treatment also rose for a second month in a row, to an estimated 7.37 million treatments at the end of August, the highest since October 2025.

To prepare for winter, Cooper announced £140m of funding for urgent care capacity. The money will support 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments. Cooper said winter would be more challenging this year and that the NHS had been preparing early. NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, and medical director Frankie Swords said there were already ominous signs of winter pressure.

Reactions were mixed. Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act but asked where the money was coming from. The Royal College of Nursing in England said the funding was 'just another sticking plaster' on a system at breaking point, and warned that nursing staff were already stretched. The King's Fund described a 'twin crisis' for the service going into winter. The main test ahead will be whether the promised plans deliver visible reductions in corridor care and whether the NHS can meet its target of treating 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.

stories.summary: A BBC World feature reports on a wave of homemade synthetic drugs in the United States, following users and recovery groups in Columbus, Ohio and Chicago. Fentanyl is now often mixed with animal tranquillisers such as xylazine and medetomidine, which can make overdoses harder to reverse with naloxone. stories.story:
The BBC World feature examines a growing supply of homemade synthetic drugs in the United States and how they are deepening the country's drug crisis. Reporters spent several days with a 48-year-old army veteran in Columbus, Ohio, who uses fentanyl and says it may be cut with other substances. The piece describes how synthetic opioids have transformed the drug market, with fentanyl estimated to be 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin and often mixed with synthetic tranquillisers.

The article sets out the scale of the problem. At its peak in 2022, around 110,000 Americans died from overdoses, mostly from opioids. Deaths have since fallen to roughly 70,000 last year, but the reporter argues the crisis is not over. Naloxone, the nasal spray sold as Narcan, has saved many lives, yet it does not work against the tranquillisers xylazine and medetomidine, which slow breathing and cause severe skin wounds.

The feature also looks at stimulant users. A recovery group leader in Columbus, Scott Sanders, says that 78% of fatal overdoses in Franklin County in the last year involved stimulants. Users buying crack may be getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioids without knowing. Through a drug-sampling programme with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, one sample tested positive for medetomidine. The piece also includes an interview with a cartel-linked fentanyl dealer in Chicago, who did not want to be identified.

The story is a long-form feature rather than a policy announcement, and it does not set out any new government measures. It highlights how drug supply is changing faster than treatment and harm-reduction tools. For readers, the key message is that the danger is shifting from single drugs to unpredictable mixtures, which makes overdoses harder to detect and reverse.

stories.headline: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base
stories.claim: A major fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta caused deaths and many injuries among military personnel.
stories.summary: A major fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta has killed and injured people, according to Canada's defence minister. Fierce winds spread flames into surrounding rural land, and many injured people were taken to hospitals, including in Edmonton. By late evening the fire was reported as held, with no evacuation order. The incident comes days before a referendum in Alberta on a process that could lead to independence.
key_points: Defence Minister David McGuinty said people were killed and injured in an incident at the base.
The fire broke out in a training area and police were called shortly after 4 p.m. on Saturday.
Many injured people were transported to hospitals, with a doctor describing the scale as overwhelming.
By 11 p.m. local authorities said the fire was being held and no evacuation order was in place.
The fire disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's Alberta independence-process referendum, with two polling stations closing early.
stories.story:
A major fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, a military training base in Alberta, has caused deaths and injuries, according to Canada's Defence Minister David McGuinty. Reports said large numbers of injured people were taken to hospitals, including in Edmonton, around 180 km away. The exact number of casualties was not immediately clear. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is involved in investigating what happened, and the minister described the situation as active and delicate.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. on Saturday 17 October following reports of a fire in a training area. Strong winds, with gusts of up to 100 km/h across parts of the province, made firefighting difficult and carried flames into the surrounding rural area. By 11 p.m. the Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. No evacuation order was issued for residents of the nearby town of Wainwright, which has about 7,000 people.

The base is one of Canada's busiest training sites, home to a manoeuvre training centre and a divisional training centre. Prime Minister Mark Carney, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and opposition leader Pierre Poilievre all issued statements of support, and Saskatchewan said it was sending help. The fire also affected advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said two polling locations closed early and ballots were moved securely.

What happens next depends on the police investigation and official casualty figures, which were still awaited at the time of reporting. Readers should expect more detail on the cause and the final toll in coming hours and days. The political timing of the fire, close to the referendum vote, is likely to be a focus of coverage.

stories.headline: Whole streets in Paris ‘devastated’ by protests, says mayor, as France demonstrations continue – Europe live
stories.claim: Violent protests across France and parts of Europe on Saturday caused major damage, with over 1,200 arrests in France.
stories.summary: Protests in France on Saturday, which began as student demonstrations over living costs and school conditions, turned violent in several cities. Buildings were attacked and set alight, including Limoges town hall, and whole streets in Paris were described as devastated by the mayor. More than 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were reportedly hurt. Violence also broke out in Milan, and peaceful protests took place in Lisbon. Authorities were waiting to see whether unrest would continue.
key_points: More than 1,200 people were arrested across France on Saturday.
Paris police arrested a record 855 people, the highest for a single event according to AFP.
Limoges town hall was largely destroyed by a fire set by masked protesters.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were hurt.
Clashes and looting also occurred in central Milan, with about 50 detained.
stories.story:
Protests in France on Saturday, which began with high school students and cost-of-living concerns, escalated into the country's worst unrest in years. While hundreds of thousands marched peacefully in many cities, violent fringe groups attacked public buildings, luxury shops and supermarkets, and targeted police. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez blamed opportunistic looters for hijacking the official demonstration.

In Paris, police arrested a record 855 people, which AFP reported was the highest ever for a single event. The city's mayor, Emmanuel Grégoire, said whole streets had been devastated, and a deputy mayor described violence unlike anything seen before. In Limoges, the town hall, a 143-year-old building, was largely lost to a fire set by masked protesters, though the prefect said on Sunday the blaze had been contained.

The protests began last month in schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris, over teacher absences and poor facilities, and later grew into a nationwide movement against inequality and weak public spending. Similar unrest occurred in Milan, where rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set fires, leaving at least two officers injured and around 50 people detained. In Lisbon, several hundred people gathered peacefully to protest housing and living costs. Authorities in France were waiting to see whether protests would continue.
stories.market_take: Prolonged unrest and rising political uncertainty could weigh on French government bonds and the CAC 40.

stories.summary: Columnist Hamish McRae says the UK economy is performing better than expected, with growth of 2.1 per cent in the year to August. He credits business resilience and AI adoption, particularly in services, rather than the government. He notes that roughly 150,000 jobs have been lost over two years and that the public sector lags on productivity. The piece is an opinion column, not a new data release.

stories.story:
Hamish McRae, writing for This Is Money, argues that the UK economy is doing better than many expect, and that this has little to do with the current government. He says growth reached 2.1 per cent in the 12 months to the end of August, a figure he regards as respectable. He attributes the improvement to the resilience of British businesses and to firms using artificial intelligence and contractors to lift output while holding back on hiring. Construction is weaker, but services, manufacturing and investment appear to be recovering, which he links to the effects of the previous chancellor's budgets gradually fading.

The column notes that around 150,000 jobs have been lost over the past two years as companies raised prices and cut payrolls in response to higher labour costs. McRae suggests AI is a particular advantage for Britain because services and knowledge-based activities are a large share of the economy. Nearly 60 per cent of UK exports are services, and about half of recent growth is coming from consultancy, law and market research, which are among the heaviest adopters of AI.

McRae is critical of the public sector, which he says has made little productivity progress since 1997, while the private sector is reported to be 42 to 45 per cent more productive. He cites a government trial involving 20,000 civil servants that suggested AI could save two weeks of work a year on admin. He argues the government could do much better.

The piece also comes ahead of the Budget on 28 October, which the article says is expected to bring tax changes. The article is a commentary, and it contains promotional material for a financial planning series and affiliate links, which are not part of the economic analysis.
stories.market_take: Stronger services growth and AI-led productivity could support UK-focused service firms ahead of the Budget.

stories.claim: Circle says it kept about 7 cents profit per dollar of revenue in H1 2026 as rival stablecoin products compete for partners.
stories.summary: Circle, the USDC stablecoin issuer, defended its business model in a blog post, saying it kept about 7 cents of net profit per dollar of revenue in the first half of 2026. Coinbase, its largest distribution partner, is backing a rival, Open USD, which shares reserve income with businesses. Circle's revenue was about $1.4 billion. The dispute centres on who receives interest from reserve assets.

stories.story:
Circle, the issuer of the USDC stablecoin, has defended its business model in a blog post by its chief commercial officer, Kash Razzaghi. He said the company kept about 7 cents in net profit for every dollar of revenue in the first half of 2026. Revenue was about $1.4 billion, while distribution and transaction costs were $819 million. The remaining $473 million covered compliance, liquidity and product development, and included roughly $214 million in stock-based compensation.

The post comes amid a dispute over who should receive interest earned on the reserves that back stablecoins. Coinbase, Circle's largest USDC distribution partner, is also a backer of Open USD, a rival launched alongside Stripe and BlackRock. Open USD allows businesses to mint and redeem stablecoins without fees and passes reserve income, minus a management fee, to participants. Other competitors, such as the Paxos-led Global Dollar Network (USDG), also share reserve income. Circle did not name Open USD directly in its post.

Circle has been seeking more distribution partners. In September, Binance bought a $100 million stake in the company under a five-year agreement that includes a fee linked to USDC held through Circle's wallet service. The company said standard redemptions remain free and typically settle within two business days, while qualifying platform customers and Circle Payments Network flows can access near-real-time redemptions at no cost.

The article's page also included a promotional line about yield on real-world asset stablecoins, which is not part of the reporting. The key question for investors is whether Circle can keep its partners as rivals offer larger shares of reserve income.
stories.market_take: Competition over reserve income could pressure Circle's margins and its distribution relationships with Coinbase.

PowerLines data show electricity prices up about 40% over five years and utilities seeking $23.1 billion in rate rises through the first three quarters of 2026. stories.story:
Fortune reports that utility bills and the data centre boom are becoming a major issue in the run-up to the November midterm elections in the United States. The article, drawing on comments from Charles Hua of the PowerLines nonprofit, argues that electricity costs could influence results in several states and in Congress, not only fuel prices linked to the Iran war.

The figures cited are substantial. US electricity prices have risen by roughly 40% on average over the past five years. Utilities requested another $23.1 billion in rate increases in the first three quarters of 2026, on track to rival the nearly $31 billion record set in 2025. Investor-owned utilities have raised their capital expenditure plans by more than 27% to at least $1.4 trillion through 2030, a large share of it for new generation, partly to serve AI data centres.

Fuel costs are also high. Regular unleaded petrol averaged $4.33 a gallon, up 42% on a year earlier, and diesel averaged $6.33, up 73%. Heating oil in September was up 74% from a year before, which campaigners warn will hit households as winter begins. The White House has backed a non-binding ratepayer pledge with hyperscale data centre firms, and some states have imposed moratoriums on data centres.

The article notes that data centres are only partly responsible for rising bills in some places, and that the link is contested. Hua said public perception that data centres are raising bills is widespread across most states. The piece suggests that utility rate requests, which public utility commissions often approve, may come under greater political scrutiny. What happens next will depend on pending rate decisions and how the election campaign develops.
stories.market_take: Pressure on utility rate cases and data centre costs could weigh on regulated utilities and affect sentiment towards AI power demand.

stories.story:
Households that rely on heating oil are struggling with a sharp rise in prices, which they link to the US-Israeli war with Iran. Several residents in the South West told the BBC they have delayed buying fuel for the winter, hoping prices would fall, and they worry that some people may not be able to heat their homes at all. The cost increases are a particular problem for rural areas, where many homes are not connected to the mains gas network.

The energy consumers minister, Polly Billington, said heating fuel costs had risen by as much as 82% since the conflict began. She said the government wanted to make sure the market worked as fairly as possible. Earlier in October, ministers promised tighter rules for the sector, measures to promote competition and clearer routes for customers to seek compensation when things go wrong. Minimum order levels, which apply to some customers, are also to be reviewed. In March, the government had already announced a £53m support package for low-income families who use heating oil.

Individual residents described the impact on their budgets. One woman in Devon said a 500-litre delivery that cost about £340 last year was now just over £600. A 76-year-old in Cornwall said she had already spent more on two deliveries this year than in previous years and expected to heat her home less. Another Cornish resident who saves £30 a month into a scheme said she could no longer afford to fill her tank.

The residents interviewed were not hopeful that regulation alone would reduce prices. The coming months will test whether the new measures and the existing support package are enough to help households through the winter, particularly those in rural areas.
stories.market_take: Higher heating oil prices and tighter regulation may affect fuel suppliers and consumer energy costs, though the effect on listed companies is likely modest.

stories.headline: Condé Nast’s UK profits drop by more than a third as sale of Vogue publisher ruled out
stories.claim: Condé Nast's UK profits fell by over a third last year, as the Newhouse family ruled out selling the publisher.
stories.summary: Condé Nast's UK arm saw pre-tax profits, excluding exceptional items, drop 36% to nearly £18m in the latest accounts. UK revenues fell 7% to £70.6m, while international revenues rose 18%, keeping total revenue almost flat at about £100m. The figures came shortly after the Newhouse family, which controls the group, ruled out a sale. Restructuring costs more than doubled to £4.3m, mostly severance.
key_points: UK pre-tax profit excluding exceptional items fell 36%, from £28m in 2024 to nearly £18m in 2025.
UK revenues dropped 7% to £70.6m, while international revenues rose 18% to £29.7m.

Restructuring costs more than doubled, from £1.9m to £4.3m, mainly severance.
The Newhouse family ruled out a sale after chief executive Roger Lynch left to lead Mattel.

stories.story:
Condé Nast's UK business reported a sharp fall in profits for last year, according to newly filed accounts. Pre-tax profit before exceptional items dropped by more than a third, from £28m in 2024 to just under £18m. The 2024 figure had been boosted by £64m from the sale of the Vogue House headquarters in London, so the comparison is flattered in the earlier year. Revenues generated in the UK fell 7% to £70.6m, but growth in international revenues of 18% to £29.7m kept total revenues close to flat at about £100m.

The company said it remains profitable in the UK and attributed the lower profit to planned investment in customised client solutions. Restructuring costs more than doubled to £4.3m, which the company said was mainly severance. Headcount barely changed, falling from 466 to 461. The company also pointed to changes in pension scheme projections and wage inflation as factors hitting profit.

The filings come days after Steven Newhouse, chair of Advance, the family holding company that controls Condé Nast, ruled out selling the group. Speculation had linked Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, who owns the Washington Post, to a possible purchase. The announcement followed the abrupt departure of chief executive Roger Lynch, who was hired in 2019 to turn the business around and is moving to become boss of the toymaker Mattel.

Lynch had earlier described Google's AI Summaries as a further blow to traditional search traffic, saying Google searches were no longer a meaningful driver of the business and made up only about a quarter of visits to its websites last year. Seven large titles, including Vogue, GQ and the New Yorker, account for 85% of group revenues. The highest-paid director, the company's most senior executive outside the US who resigned last August, took home more than £1.3m. Earlier this year the group also announced plans to close the women's health magazine Self after 47 years.
stories.market_take: Private company with no listed shares, so the results have little direct market impact beyond signals for the wider magazine and publishing sector.

The author points to strong 2026 returns for tech funds and the Nasdaq-100 and argues that most Americans do not own the stocks benefiting from AI. stories.story:
A commentary piece published in Fortune argues that the United States should introduce a scheme called Innovation Accounts to give ordinary adults a stake in the country's AI boom. The author notes that tech-focused hedge funds returned around 27% on average in the first half of 2026 and that the Nasdaq-100 rose about 20% over the same period, while many Americans do not own the shares that have driven these gains. The writer suggests that accounts seeded with money, for example $1,000 or $5,000, could be placed in a technology-stock index and paid out at intervals. The idea is presented as an extension of Trump Accounts, which are set up under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to give children born between 2025 and 2028 a $1,000 government-funded stake in the market, and of Alaska's Permanent Fund, which pays residents an annual dividend from oil revenues.

The piece gives rough costs: about $270 billion for universal $1,000 accounts for adults, or about $190 billion if limited to households with wealth below $500,000. It suggests targeting through triggers such as sector-specific unemployment, and a pilot of $5 billion could seed one million accounts at $5,000 each. Funding could come from government or philanthropy, and the author proposes that AI founders, early employees and investors could be a source of capital.

The article is clearly marked as opinion and not as the publication's own view. Critics would likely raise questions about funding sources, the risks of concentrated tech holdings and whether government-backed accounts are workable. The author acknowledges that index returns are not guaranteed and that the scheme would not replace lost jobs. No government has committed to the proposal.
