stories.story:
Yemen's internationally recognised government says Houthi forces fired two missiles at Aden International Airport on Friday. The information minister, Moammar al-Eryani, said the projectiles landed near the runway about 500 metres from an aircraft that was getting ready to take off. He said everyone on board was safe and described the strikes as a serious breach of international law. The attack followed a deadly assault on the presidential palace in Aden the previous day. Aden is the seat of the government.

The Houthis said in a statement attributed to a military source that they had targeted Saudi forces' command headquarters at Badr camp in Aden province, along with a weapons depot. The fighting is part of a wider conflict that has reignited between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned group. Government forces said they had made significant territorial gains in eastern Marib province with air support, and claimed to have killed more than 430 Houthi fighters in 24 hours. In Taiz, a major front line, they said they had repelled several large attacks.

The Houthis have encircled Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, by cutting its main road to Aden, causing displacement and a worsening humanitarian crisis. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said it had shot down missiles and drones over Riyadh and other parts of the kingdom. Riyadh accuses Iran of arming and training the Houthis, a charge Tehran rejects.

The war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa. A 2022 UN-backed truce had largely halted fighting, but tensions rose after the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi ports and shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in July. Since September the group has pushed further on the western coast, taking Mocha and Mayyun Island. The latest strikes raise the risk of wider escalation in a key Red Sea shipping corridor.

The article focuses on people who have been kept apart for nearly three years, often because of injuries, medical needs or the difficulty of crossing into Egypt.

Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, left Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment after an Israeli strike on a tower near their home in Nuseirat injured the whole family. Her daughter Nour suffered a fractured skull and brain bleeding and spent about 33 days in intensive care. Wijdan's husband, Hatem, who was also injured, remains in Gaza, displaced in a tent, and contact is difficult because of poor internet. Wijdan has no regular income, struggles to pay for her daughter's medication and school transport, and says she is exhausted.

Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old photojournalist, left Gaza in April 2024 after his home was destroyed. His fiancee, Ola, could not reach southern Gaza to cross into Egypt when Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah, and the two have still not married. He describes loneliness and guilt, and says he has lost sleep since arriving in Egypt.

The piece cites Gaza health ministry figures of at least 73,783 Palestinians killed and 174,738 wounded since the war began. It also refers to an independent UN inquiry that found Israel continues to commit genocide by targeting children, a conclusion Israel has rejected. The article is a human-interest feature rather than a news report on a policy change, and it does not describe any new negotiation or border opening that would alter these families' situations.

stories.headline: Decades after apartheid, South Africans seek justice for crimes of the past
stories.claim: Sharpeville families pursue a class action over the 1960 massacre, challenging an apartheid-era indemnity law in court.
stories.summary: Families of people killed by police at the 1960 Sharpeville massacre are seeking justice and reparations decades later. In September they filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961, which they say still blocks claims. The case is part of a wider wave of efforts to reopen apartheid-era killings, including inquests into Albert Luthuli, the Cradock Four and Steve Biko. A government inquiry into shelved prosecution recommendations is due to report in December.
key_points: At least 69 people were shot by police at Sharpeville on 21 March 1960 while protesting against pass laws.
Families filed a High Court application in September 2026 challenging the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961.

Inquests into the Cradock Four and Steve Biko have been reopened.

stories.story:
Relatives of victims of the Sharpeville massacre in South Africa are pressing for justice more than six decades after police opened fire on a crowd of anti-apartheid protesters on 21 March 1960. At least 69 people were killed in the shooting, which took place during a demonstration against the pass laws that restricted where Black South Africans could live and work. Paulina Mathinye, whose father was killed that day, says the state has not properly recognised his role, and that the loss left her family struggling for decades.

In September the families and their lawyers filed an application at the Gauteng High Court. They are challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961, an apartheid-era law that the lawyers say still prevents them from seeking legal redress. If the court finds the law unconstitutional and certifies a class action for survivors and dependants, individual claims for damages could follow. It is unclear whether any perpetrators are still alive.

The Sharpeville case is one of several recent efforts to revisit apartheid-era crimes. A court last year ruled that Chief Albert Luthuli, South Africa's first Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was beaten to death by apartheid police in 1967, overturning an earlier finding that he had died after being struck by a train. Inquests into the 1985 killings of the Cradock Four and the 1977 death in custody of Steve Biko have also been reopened, with Biko's family hoping for a clear finding of murder.

Separately, President Cyril Ramaphosa set up a formal inquiry last year to examine whether hundreds of Truth and Reconciliation Commission prosecution recommendations were deliberately shelved, including whether a secret deal shielded former apartheid leaders. Its findings are due in December. Lawyers involved describe the cases as a chance to pursue truth and accountability before it is too late.

stories.story:
Demand for rooftop solar power is booming in the Philippines as the war involving Iran has pushed up energy prices. Households that once paid about $150 a month for electricity have seen bills rise to as much as $220, and many are now installing panels as a longer-term hedge against price swings. One family quoted in the report expects the system to pay for itself in about five years.

The figures are striking. A report by the think tank Ember found that rooftop panels nearly doubled in the country from early 2025. Government trade data cited in the article show $407m of panel imports in the first months of the war, from March to May, making the Philippines the largest single overseas buyer for that period, apart from the Netherlands, which redistributes panels across Europe. One solar supplier says it now sets up 25 to 30 systems a month and faces a 30-day wait.

The Philippines already had some of the highest electricity costs in Southeast Asia, and it relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power. A weaker peso, which has hit a record low of more than 63 to the dollar, makes these imports dearer. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in late March. Public anger has also grown over charges for system losses, which include illegal connections.

The upfront cost of a system remains out of reach for many. A new government loan scheme for rooftop installations is limited to public sector workers. Officials are relying on large projects, including a planned 3,500-hectare solar farm north of Manila, which is expected to supply 850 megawatts to 2.4 million households once complete. Some consumers warn that such projects could take years, leaving them exposed to rising bills in the meantime.

Reports that the UK Chancellor, John Healey, may raise the surcharge on bank profits have prompted warnings from the City that households would bear the cost. The Telegraph reports that the government is considering increasing the surcharge on profits above £100m from 3pc to 8pc. Analysts at UBS argue that banks would pass the extra tax on to customers through higher mortgage rates and lower savings rates, and that the measure could bring in less revenue than expected while discouraging investment. They also note that the average mortgage rate has already climbed from 4.9pc before the war in Iran to 5.88pc, according to Moneyfacts.

The market reaction was concentrated in the banking sector. Lloyds and NatWest fell more than 2pc on Friday and were the weakest performers on the FTSE 100. UBS said NatWest would be hardest hit, with an annual cost of £263m at a 6pc rate. Shore Capital estimated that an 8pc surcharge would cut earnings at Lloyds and NatWest by about 6pc, against roughly 2pc for Barclays and 1pc for HSBC. It also suggested that a higher allowance, perhaps £500m, could help smaller lenders and fintechs.

The wider market was less affected. The FTSE 100 was on course for its best week since April, and the defensive healthcare sector was set for a gain of nearly 5pc after a sell-off in AI stocks. The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, said second-round inflation effects from the Iran energy shock appeared limited so far. Other voices added to the criticism: the ICAEW warned that the tax system is damaging growth, a housing lender reported slower sales, and TheCityUK said a sector-specific tax would hurt investor confidence. Jamie Dimon of JP Morgan had earlier warned that his bank could pull investment from the UK if the government became hostile to banks.

No decision has been announced. The measure is still under consideration ahead of the Budget, and the final shape, including any change to the profit allowance, will determine how much banks are affected.

stories.story:
A City AM column examines whether changes to UK tax rules have made the Premier League less attractive to overseas footballers. The writer notes that Premier League clubs spent almost £3.5bn on transfer fees in the summer window, and that there were many large transfers between English clubs, which is unusual compared with earlier windows. The author also links recruitment to the league's profit and sustainability rules, pointing to the Manchester City case as a reason clubs are keen to manage spending carefully.

The main argument concerns tax. Under the old system, players who played matches in Europe could claim Overseas Workday Relief on part of their salary, and they could shelter non-UK income under the Remittance Basis for up to 15 years. Since April 2025 the Foreign Income and Gains regime has replaced the Remittance Basis. It offers a full exemption on non-UK income and gains, which is more generous, but only lasts four tax years. OWR can now be claimed for four years, but only up to £300,000 a year, which the writer says weakens its value for players earning more than that weekly.

The result, according to the column, is a shorter but potentially more generous window for newcomers, and less long-term certainty than the Remittance Basis gave. The writer suggests that a player may plan to leave after about three seasons, and that clubs may need to consider this when recruiting. The column also raises the prospect of the government relaxing the rules ahead of the Budget to keep the league competitive, though it acknowledges that public sympathy for highly paid footballers is likely to be limited. No government response is reported in the piece.

The surcharge was introduced a decade ago, cut to 3% under Rishi Sunak when corporation tax rose, and the overall rate on banks rose to 28% in 2023. stories.summary: Jersey Deputy Louise Doublet has said cost-of-living pressures were not considered when the government ended a trial of free fruit in four primary schools. The education minister ended the scheme due to low uptake and wastage. Fruit is now to be included in the government's hot school meal programme. Doublet called for more investment in healthy, locally grown food.
key_points: A free fruit trial in four Jersey primary schools has ended after running since 2024.
The education minister cited low consumption and a lot of wastage.
Fruit will now be included in the government's hot school meal programme, announced in September.
Deputy Louise Doublet says the scheme's cost-of-living benefits were not measured.
Doublet supports extending the funded school meals, which come from Apetito Limited.
The government has yet to respond to a request for comment.
stories.story:
A Jersey politician has called for more funding for food in schools, arguing that the government did not properly consider cost-of-living pressures when it ended a trial of free fruit in primary schools. Since 2024, children in four primary schools had been able to take apples, bananas and other fruit under the pilot. Deputy Louise Doublet said ending it at a time when living costs are still rising had been hard for some families.

Education minister Catherine Curtis ended the trial because too few children were eating the fruit and a lot of it was being wasted. The government announced in September that fresh fruit would instead be included in the hot school meals programme for government primary schools. Curtis said parents had asked for fruit to be added to that programme. The topic was debated in the States Assembly on 29 September.

Doublet accepted the minister's evidence that the trial had not significantly increased fruit and vegetable consumption, but said the scheme's wider benefit for family budgets had not been measured. She said she would like to see more investment in healthy food, especially locally grown produce. Asked about the contract with the UK firm Apetito, which supplies the hot meals, she said it was the best available option and that the meals are frozen rather than preserved artificially.

The Government of Jersey was approached for comment, and the BBC report does not include a response. The story is a local policy debate rather than a national or market-moving issue.

stories.headline: ‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?
stories.claim: IMF meeting in Bangkok warns global resilience is fragile, with high debt and AI-bubble risks.
stories.summary: Coverage of the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok says the global economy has held up better than feared despite high oil prices and the Iran conflict. The IMF warns that energy subsidies cost 0.5% of global GDP and cannot last, and that advanced-economy debt will rise from 108% to 115% of GDP in five years. Georgieva warned that AI expectations could outrun productivity gains. The G20 meeting issued no communique, and US Treasury Secretary Bessent did not attend.
key_points: The IMF says energy support measures have cost about 0.5% of global GDP and many governments cannot sustain them.
Advanced-economy debt is projected to rise from 108% of GDP last year to 115% in five years.
Bond yields have risen to their highest levels in decades, partly reflecting fiscal worries.
Georgieva warned that AI expectations could run ahead of productivity gains, risking a near-term disappointment.
The G20 finance meeting produced no communique, and US Treasury Secretary Bessent did not attend.
The UK chancellor chaired the G20 meeting and the UK received praise for its deficit plan.
stories.story:
Policymakers from more than 100 countries met in Bangkok for the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting, where the mood was one of surprising resilience. Growth has held up, helped by AI investment, and stock markets have not crashed despite high oil prices and the conflict involving Iran. Analysts quoted at the event said countries were defying the expected economic damage.

The IMF cautioned that this resilience has a cost and may not last. Its World Economic Outlook says energy support measures have cost about 0.5% of global GDP, and it urges governments to use temporary, targeted help rather than broad subsidies. Some countries have already begun to phase out support. The fund also warns that public finances in rich countries are strained, with advanced-economy debt projected to rise from 108% of GDP last year to 115% in five years. Bond yields have climbed to their highest levels in decades, partly reflecting worries about government borrowing.

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva urged governments, including the United States, to rebuild fiscal buffers before the next shock. A separate concern is that AI expectations may be running ahead of productivity gains. Georgieva said this could lead to near-term disappointment, and Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh was quoted as optimistic about long-term gains from AI.

The meeting also highlighted geopolitical divisions. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent did not travel to Bangkok, and the UK chancellor chaired the G20 finance meeting instead. No communique was issued, which reflects the difficulty of reaching multilateral agreement. The UK, which takes over the G20 presidency next year, was praised by the IMF for its deficit reduction plan, although its bond yields have not fallen as much as hoped.
stories.market_take: Rising sovereign bond yields and the warning on AI valuations could weigh on bond and equity markets if sentiment shifts.

stocks.reason: High public debt and fiscal worries keep upward pressure on long-term yields.

stories.headline: The collapse of web coding gigs is getting ugly — AI takes over routine website development jobs, and business owners are very happy with its job so far
stories.claim: A Bluehost survey finds many US business owners now build websites with AI tools, while freelance web development work has fallen sharply.
stories.summary: A survey of 201 American entrepreneters commissioned by Bluehost found that 53% had adopted AI website builders instead of professional developers. Respondents reported average savings of about $850 and roughly 32 working hours per project. Freelance listings for PHP, WordPress and HTML work fell by between 55% and 59% since 2024. Most adopters were satisfied, though few published AI output unchanged. The sample is small, so the findings carry notable uncertainty.
key_points: 53% of surveyed US business owners said they had adopted AI website builders.
Adopters reported average savings of $850 and about 32 working hours per project.
Freelance PHP postings fell 59%, WordPress 58% and HTML 55%, according to the report.
97% of adopters reported at least moderate satisfaction, and 72% strong approval.
Only 9% published AI-generated sites without changes; 61% revised content and 60% altered visuals.
The survey covers 201 people, with a margin of about 6.9 percentage points at 95% confidence.
stories.story:
Freelance website development work has dropped sharply since 2024, and a new survey suggests artificial intelligence is a major reason. Bluehost, a web hosting company, commissioned research among 201 American entrepreneurs involved in decisions about their firms' online operations. It found that 53% had used AI website builders rather than hiring professional developers.

Adopters said the tools saved them an average of $850 and around 32 working hours compared with commissioning a developer or agency. Among them, 85% said their sites would have been built differently without AI. Hosting and domain setup were the tasks respondents were least willing to hand over to AI, at 21%.

The report also tracked freelance job listings. PHP vacancies fell 59%, WordPress assignments fell 58% and HTML roles fell 55%, which the article describes as steeper than several other freelance categories. Even among those who had not used AI builders, 71% said they would consider them for future projects.

Satisfaction was high, but adopters remained involved. Only 9% published AI output without edits, and 54% preferred to review every change, while 30% were comfortable letting AI act without approval. Just half said they would tell customers that their site was AI-made. Of AI users, 94% kept using AI for other business tasks after launch. The survey is small, so its estimates should be treated with caution.
stories.market_take: Pressure on freelance platforms and web development service providers could grow if AI builders keep gaining share.

stories.claim: Cloudflare has bought Deno, and creator Ryan Dahl is moving to work on open source Cloudflare Workers.
stories.summary: Cloudflare has acquired Deno, the JavaScript runtime startup founded by Node.js creator Ryan Dahl, in an acquihire that brings Dahl and 12 colleagues in-house. Deno will receive fixes and security patches for a year before development ends. Dahl's team plans to build a standalone runtime from his celld project and Cloudflare's workerd. Dahl says Node.js is the wrong choice for building servers. The move leaves fewer independent runtimes in the market.
key_points: Cloudflare bought Deno, which had about 400,000 monthly users as of August.
Cloudflare will maintain Deno for a year, then end its development.
Dahl and 12 Deno staff will work on Cloudflare Workers.
The team plans to merge celld with workerd into a standalone runtime.
Dahl says Deno became too similar to Node.js to gain ground.
Deno had raised $21 million from Sequoia in 2022.
stories.story:
Cloudflare has purchased Deno, the server-side JavaScript runtime startup founded by Ryan Dahl, who also created Node.js. The deal is effectively an acquihire, bringing Dahl and 12 Deno colleagues into Cloudflare to work on its Workers platform. Cloudflare will continue to supply bug fixes and security patches for Deno for another year, after which its development will end.

Dahl said Deno struggled to win users against Node.js. Deno, first released in 2018, was intended as a fix for what he saw as mistakes in Node. Over time, though, it had to become more compatible with Node, which left it as an alternative implementation. Sequoia backed the company with $21 million in 2022, and the project had around 400,000 monthly users as of August.

Dahl's new focus is a runtime that can be self-hosted, not just used on Cloudflare's infrastructure. He released celld in August as an open-source version of Cloudflare's Durable Objects, and the team plans to merge it with Cloudflare's workerd into a standalone JavaScript and WebAssembly runtime. The article says this could need around 300 KB of memory per instance, far less than Node or Deno typically use.

The article notes that the deal reduces the number of independent runtimes available, following Anthropic's recent acquisition of Bun. The MIT-licensed Deno project is still looking for a new home, possibly with the OpenJS Foundation. The wider effect will depend on whether the Cloudflare-backed runtime gains adoption.
stories.market_take: The deal is small and Cloudflare's share price is unlikely to move much on it alone.

stocks.reason: Adds an experienced runtime team to its Workers platform.

stories.headline: 'Remarkably close to the minimum permitted by physics': this superconducting memory bit runs at an estimated 5x the limit, but at -269°C the fridge shrinks its claimed million-fold edge over today’s chips considerably
stories.claim: Hebrew University researchers report a superconducting memory bit operating near five times Landauer's limit, with significant caveats.
stories.summary: Physicists at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem report that a single superconducting vortex can store a bit at about five times the Landauer limit, the theoretical minimum energy cost of erasing a bit. The result was published in Nature Communications in September. The device works only at liquid-helium temperatures and the figure is partly based on simulations rather than direct measurement. The paper's peer review was unusually contested. Critics say speed and cooling costs limit practical value.
key_points: The team estimates a working bit runs at about five times Landauer's limit at 150 kHz.
The device uses a 55-nanometre niobium film cooled to 4.2 kelvin.
The erasure figure comes from simulations anchored to measurements of continuous driving.
A reviewer disputed whether work was measured or inferred, and the authors declined extra checks.
Stored bits can hop spontaneously, holding data for well under a millisecond in the most efficient wells.
Cooling costs are not included, and the approach is far slower than superconducting logic chips.
stories.story:
Physicists at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem say they have used a single superconducting vortex to store a bit at roughly five times the theoretical minimum energy cost of erasing one. That minimum, known as Landauer's limit, was set by IBM physicist Rolf Landauer in 1961. The work was published in Nature Communications on 24 September and promoted by the university on 11 October.

The experiment used a 55-nanometre niobium film cooled to 4.2 kelvin. A current moved a magnetic vortex between two nearby resting positions, which act as zero and one. The team measured energy lost during continuous back-and-forth driving using a magnetic sensor on a glass probe. The five-times figure for true erasure, however, was estimated with simulations, and the authors state that their method is not the same as the standard erasure protocol.

The publication has drawn criticism. One of three peer reviewers recommended against the final version, saying that work was inferred rather than observed. The authors declined requests for further experiments, citing drift in their scanning equipment. Another reviewer supported publication, while a third said the technique was ill-suited to erasure at useful speeds.

The article also highlights practical limits. The estimate applies at 150 kHz, far slower than superconducting logic chips that have run at 6 GHz for over a decade. The cost of refrigeration to 4.2 kelvin is not counted. The most efficient wells can hold data for well under a millisecond, so they are not yet suitable for durable storage. The contribution is mainly an energy accounting result, and vortex memory itself is not new.
